fix(computer): blank selectors prevent computer tool calls (#155072)

Closes #155061

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes computer calls failing when a model fills optional target, node, and environmentId selectors with empty or whitespace-only strings.

## User Impact

Blank selectors resolve exactly like omitted selectors. Existing target selection, pairing, environment attachment, and authorization remain unchanged. Nonblank unknown nodes and invalid targets still fail.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prepare only these three blank string fields before argument validation. Normalizing only inside the resolver was too late: an empty target failed the existing enum validation first. The tool uses one preparer for model calls and direct execution; the model-facing schema is unchanged. Nonblank values are not rewritten.

## Evidence

An isolated Gateway, scripted local OpenAI-compatible provider, and approved fake paired computer node exercised real model turns and node RPC transport. The node returns a synthetic one-pixel screenshot, not a real desktop capture.

- Main production source at 52c7502c8613: all-empty selectors fail target enum validation; omitted selectors and an explicit valid node both return the screenshot.
- Candidate: all-empty, whitespace-only, omitted, and explicit valid-node selectors each complete one computer call with zero failures on the same node.
- Unknown nonblank node still fails resolution; target=foo still fails enum validation.
- The new preparation regression fails against main at schema validation. The candidate node-resolution suite passes 20/20 (18.27 seconds whole-command wall; blank preparation case 2ms).

Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/computer-tool.node-resolution.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`.

No schema, permission, or configuration changes. No project-wide test suite was run.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

fix(agents): replies stall when a chat is marked read as a turn starts (#158209)

* fix(agents): replies stall when a chat is marked read as a turn starts

The durable context-engine turn outbox ran its SQLite on the host thread. When a worker transaction, such as the read marker from sessions.patch, held the write lock while waiting on the host for its commit grant, the host's busy wait stalled both until the busy timeout, about 10 s per Control UI turn.

Run the outbox in the agent database worker through openOpenClawAgentSqliteWorkerStore. A run's start recovers, checks and admits in one worker transaction; acceptance commits before the closed-range read and publication; engine.commitTurn stays outside any transaction; the lazy outbox DDL is recorded once per connection. The transcript recorder settles its admission write before dispatch, rejects when it fails, and starts a write reported inside a session write lane detached so it queues behind that lane.

* fix(agents): await turn admission before provider dispatch

fix: automations rejects disabled failure alerts (#158325)

Closes #158224

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes: agents cannot create intentionally silent jobs when they pass the documented `failureAlert: false` value.

## User Impact
Agents can add and update jobs with disabled failure alerts, without changing scheduler behavior or requiring a migration.

## Why This Change Was Made
The model-facing schema described false but only allowed objects. It now accepts the false sentinel alongside the existing policy object. The false branch has an explicit boolean type so Codex app-server preserves it. Ordinary tool-argument recovery is unchanged: string "false", zero, and null recover to false just as they do for other boolean tool fields. Restricted-provider projections retain their existing object representation and disable-policy description; this does not expand those providers' schema dialect.

## Evidence
- Isolated Gateway on baseline: a scripted provider submitted the issue's disabled, future-at job; automations rejected it with `job.failureAlert: must be object`. The same job succeeded through `cron.add` and retained false.
- Fixed Gateway: the same model tool call created the disabled job; automations get read back false. Object and omitted policies succeeded; the invalid string "invalid" was rejected. Update with false succeeded. The disabled job's run history remained empty.
- Focused input schema, output contract, cron protocol validators, and Gemini cleaner suites passed (four shards, 40.98s). The input contract also exercises the real argument validator for add/update.
- No Gateway protocol or version changes. Full suites are left to CI.
- Generated prompt snapshots refreshed: +360 schema characters, confined to the failureAlert union; only derived counts and hashes change elsewhere.
- Codex source inspected: `codex-rs/tools/src/json_schema.rs:110-111` lowers const to enum; lines 121-130 infer string for a typeless enum, while lines 114/144 preserve an explicit boolean type. The false branch now uses standard `{type:"boolean",const:false}` everywhere, without a provider-specific schema.
- Final typed-sentinel checks: 38 input-schema tests and 3 Codex thread schema-boundary tests passed (42.99s across two shards); prompt snapshots current (7 files). Live scripted Gateway add/get/update retained false, object/omitted controls succeeded, invalid string rejected, disabled run history empty.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

## What Problem This Solves

SecretRef builder dry runs could accept an unsupported config target that the identical committing command rejected.

- Real CLI comparison through `pnpm openclaw`, with isolated home/state/config and a synthetic file provider, against main `d43d2d3be42b` and this change integrated with that main.

Config bytes stayed unchanged for all rejected commands and previews.
- Control `gateway.auth.password`: preview and committing write both exited 0 on baseline and candidate; preview left config bytes unchanged and the committing control saved the reference.
- The regression invokes the registered CLI, checks invalid preview/write rejection and unchanged config bytes, and retains a valid preview control.
- Focused command `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/config-cli.builder-schema.integration.test.ts src/cli/config-cli.integration.test.ts src/cli/config-cli.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 292 tests passed across three files, 31.64 seconds wall; regression test 790 ms. fix: allow session deletion of cron runs hidden from listings (#158212)

Closes #158180

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes `sessions delete` reporting `not_found` for persisted cron run sessions that `sessions list` displays.

## User Impact

Operators can delete or archive an explicitly named cron run session without using a raw Gateway RPC. General Gateway session listings continue to hide cron runs. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Lifecycle commands now use the existing `sessions.describe` keyed lookup rather than searching paginated display listings. The Gateway remains authoritative for session identity, main-session protection, archive state, and deletion. This removes the pagination resolver rather than changing listing visibility.

## Evidence

- Built an isolated Gateway and ran a real cron job against a scripted local provider. Interrupted a held provider request and restarted the Gateway, leaving a persisted `running` cron run row.
- Before: the CLI listed the exact `:run:` key, but `sessions delete <key> --agent main --yes --json` returned `status: "not_found"`; the row remained listed. `sessions.describe` returned its durable identity.
- After rebuilding: the same delete command returned `status: "deleted"`; the key disappeared from both CLI output and SQLite `session_nodes`.
- Controls: an ordinary session deleted successfully; a nonexistent key remained `not_found`; Gateway `sessions.list` still hid the persisted cron run before deletion.
- Focused lifecycle suite: 32 tests passed (1.97 seconds command wall time, 978 ms Vitest duration). The new cron regression failed on the baseline resolver with `not_found` and passed with the fix.
- Baseline full build and candidate runtime build passed. Repository-wide tests were not run locally.

fix: model pickers start in alphabetical order (#158130)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the first model list after Gateway startup falling back to alphabetical order, then switching to provider catalog order after refresh.

## User Impact

The web and terminal pickers start with the existing catalog owner's ranking. The selected model remains first. No configuration, protocol, schema, or model-selection policy changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The captured startup publication bypassed ranking: registry rows reached the visibility comparator without provider-order metadata. Startup now uses the same manifest ranks and `appendUnknown: false` policy as the full catalog builder. Unknown rows retain the existing alphabetical fallback instead of acquiring a temporary startup rank.

Manifest ranking also remains authoritative when explicit configured rows overlap it, matching the full catalog builder. The earlier description of authored configuration order was inaccurate and has been corrected; this fix must not invent a different startup ordering policy.

## Evidence

- A built baseline and candidate ran with an isolated Gateway and a synthetic installed provider manifest declaring `z-strong`, `m-current`, `a-small`; explicit configuration deliberately listed the same models in the opposite order. The selected model was `m-current`.
- Baseline web picker immediately after restart: Current, Small, Strong. The same open picker later changed to Current, Strong, Small.
- Candidate web picker immediately after restart: Current, Strong, Small. The rebuilt TUI also showed Current, Strong, Small on first open and after another 10 seconds; in this fixture its first open occurred after the baseline had already refreshed, so the browser capture establishes the before/after defect.
- Four regression cases exercise both the startup producer and the actual full-refresh catalog builder: manifest-only, overlapping configured/manifest rows, unknown captured rows, and configured-only unknown rows. Both publications must match the same independent expected ordering. The complete 15-test suite passed (37.59 seconds wall; four cases total 1.25 seconds).
- The original manifest startup regression failed on the pre-fix implementation with alphabetical results. Existing route and capability-inheritance checks still pass.
- The three affected agent-command thinking-capability cases also pass (20.45 seconds wall). An obsolete manifest-loader invocation-count assertion was removed rather than repinned; the actual provider, model, and supported-effort checks remain.
- The 14 static-startup cases also pass (19.30 seconds wall) with the real manifest reader retained in their existing catalog mock.
- All 71 existing agent-command tests pass (116.78 seconds wall) with the captured manifest fixture reusable by startup and selection.
- A hosted visible-yield/reset failure was not reproduced locally: the same two-test file passed 3/3 runs on merge-base `9e5c2e245841` and 3/3 on this PR head. Attribution remains unresolved; these passes do not establish a shared flake. One bounded diagnostic rerun was authorized. That attempt ended with only two cancelled jobs and no failed assertions or steps; the separately authorized infrastructure rerun completed green. The original failure attribution remains unresolved.
- No full local suite was run.

fix(telegram): preserve status tables with partial streaming (#155088)

Closes #152651

## What Problem This Solves
Telegram `/status` loses its native table when partial streaming is enabled: the stream finalizes the authored plain fallback before the structured presentation reaches Telegram's renderer.

## User Impact
Rich-enabled Telegram accounts retain the native status table in one finalized reply. Partial updates, ordinary text replies, and authored rich-disabled fallback keep their existing behavior. Unsupported control labels remain present exactly once.

## Why This Change Was Made
Render the final presentation through Telegram's existing canonical renderer before finalizing the existing preview. Preserve the exact dropped-control suffix across payload copies rather than introducing another renderer or send path. The transcript-mirror factory moves unchanged to the session owner to respect the delivery module's line cap.

Related earlier implementation: #152766. Contributor commits are preserved. No configuration, permissions, storage, public API, or other-channel changes.

## Evidence
- Baseline `ddcd52d5bffdf570aeb76c3d422236702f99415f`: the contributor's dispatch regression cases produced **8 failures / 1 pass**. Rich status and mixed-control cases retained plain text without the native table; rich-disabled authored fallback passed.
- Candidate `b603dde18d10`: the corresponding **9 dispatch cases passed**, plus **9 lane/presentation cases** and **2 current-main transcript cases**. The dispatch run took 20.33 seconds in Vitest (22.45 seconds including the runner, one worker).
- Integration preserves current main's test consolidation rather than restoring its deleted generic draft suite. The old recovery test fabricated a partial dispatch turn and bypassed dropped-label/truncation selection; it was removed rather than claiming it proved a reachable recovery flow. Presentation and dropped-label regressions remain.
- Candidate runtime was rebuilt with `qaRuntime`, not copied from another checkout.
- **Telegram Test Server, candidate exact head:** a Convex-leased QA user sent registered `/status` with `richMessages: true` and partial streaming. TDLib recorded one native `messageRichMessage` containing `pageBlockTable`; Telegram Web displayed the table shown below.
- **Normal reply control:** one streamed `/v1/responses` inference request to the local scripted `qa/test-model` fixture produced one `STATUS_STREAM_NORMAL_OK` reply. Neither `/status` command required a model inference request.
- **Streaming-off control:** after changing the isolated account to streaming off, `/status` produced one native table. Three user actions yielded exactly three bot messages, with no duplicate final messages.
- The screenshots use UTC and a synthetic model name, and show only the fixture reply. All six test messages were deleted under the lease, the specific browser session was terminated, and the runner exited successfully.

There is **no claimed live-before screenshot**. Current main `ab68eb892c96` could not complete `qaRuntime` because of an unrelated `INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT` error involving `transcript-visible-record.ts`. The original merge base `ddcd52d5bffd` built, but its captured Telegram plugin repeatedly failed to start the isolated polling worker (`telegram-ingress-worker.runtime.js` was missing). fix(agents): restore admitted optional plugin tools in Codex runs (#157840)

Fixes #157665

## What Problem This Solves

Codex runs admitted with an optional plugin tool through `toolsAlsoAllow` silently omit that tool from their dynamic catalog.

## User Impact

The admitted plugin's optional tool is available to that run. Other plugins' optional tools remain unavailable, and runs without a grant gain no optional tools. No configuration or permission changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Host supplies the Gateway-admitted grant when constructing tools. It captures a detached, frozen owner and tool-name list before invoking plugin code, and excludes the shared grant from plugin harness handoffs (including finalization). Harness-supplied options cannot replace this authority.

## Evidence

Real isolated Gateway runs used fixture plugins and a **scripted Codex app-server**, not a paid model. The calling plugin requested its own optional tool through the public `api.runtime.subagent.run({toolsAlsoAllow: [...]})` API; no fabricated grant was injected into those runs.

| Control | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Main `0814bf64d88`, grant admitted, real Codex adapter | `alpha_optional_tool` absent from `thread/start.dynamicTools` |
| Candidate, same admitted request and real Codex adapter | `openclaw.alpha_optional_tool` present; foreign `beta_optional_tool` absent |
| Candidate, no grant | Neither optional tool appears |
| Scripted Codex calls admitted alpha, then foreign beta | Alpha returns success; beta returns `Unknown OpenClaw tool` with `success:false` |
| Gateway selects a malicious fixture harness | No grant exposed at handoff. Replacing its attempt grant and supplying a foreign grant to `createToolSurface`, then adding names and rebuilding, does not admit beta; alpha remains executable. |

Redacted transport output from the candidate after merging main:

```json
{"id":"proof-alpha","result":{"contentItems":[{"type":"inputText","text":"alpha_optional_tool-ok"}],"success":true}}
{"id":"proof-beta","result":{"contentItems":[{"type":"inputText","text":"Unknown OpenClaw tool: beta_optional_tool"}],"success":false}}
```

The completed Gateway run recorded `successfulToolNames: ["alpha_optional_tool"]` and `status: "ok"`.

The authority regression first failed on the contributor head when the original grant's owner/list and the attempt property were mutated after Host capture, then passed with immutable capture. Focused coverage includes the authority tests, plugin handoff/finalization tests, coding-tool construction, and Codex dynamic-tool construction (422 tests passed before and after merging main).

Test cost: `host-capability.grant-authority.test.ts` contains 3 tests; the retained single-file shard took **9.82 s**, and the standalone cold run took **50.65 s** (single test worker). In [CI run 36131257040, job `checks-node-changed-compact-large-32`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36131257040/job/108060371893), all three authority tests passed (607 ms + 335 ms + 257 ms = **1.199 s** test execution). The containing multi-file job lasted **465 s** before fail-fast cancellation caused by an unrelated models-list failure; that duration includes setup and other tests, not just this file.

Codex dependency source was personally inspected at [`0a2eb4696c26`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/0a2eb4696c26ac33204bcd255721ab30220a4774): [thread creation consumes dynamic tools](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0a2eb4696c26ac33204bcd255721ab30220a4774/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L1448-L1498), and [dynamic calls carry namespace, tool, and arguments](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0a2eb4696c26ac33204bcd255721ab30220a4774/codex-rs/app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs#L1085-L1111).

fix: keep model pickers usable during provider sign-in (#158132)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: signing in to a provider briefly empties an already-open model picker and replaces its choices with “Loading models…” or “Checking models...”.

## User Impact

Existing choices stay visible and usable in Control UI chat, New Session, and the terminal picker while provider discovery refreshes. Changes to model restrictions, operator roles, or catalog mode still retire the previous choices. This does not change how soon a newly connected provider's models are discovered.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every config commit previously retired model choices, including the auth/provider config written during sign-in. The Gateway now compares selection policies before sending the existing retirement signal. The web and terminal catalog caches treat ordinary config notifications as refreshes; explicit selection-policy changes still clear them.

The comparison reuses the model visibility and operator-policy preparation owners. No protocol, configuration, or persistence changes are required.

## Evidence

Built baseline and candidate Gateways used isolated state and a task-owned provider whose HTTP model listing was held for eight seconds. The sign-in action was Settings → Connect provider → API key → Save, with chat and New Session pickers already open.

- Baseline: the open chat picker lost its choices and displayed the blocking loading state; the captured transition began 309 ms after Save.
- Candidate: neither web picker displayed “Loading models…”. The terminal PTY capture contained no “Checking models...” frame while sign-in and discovery ran. Existing choices remained visible, and discovered models appeared after publication.
- The held-catalog web regression fails against the original invalidation behavior because its current model list becomes empty, and passes with the fix (four tests in that file; 3.52 s wall time).
- Scoped lifecycle, terminal, and web suites: 65 tests passed; 34.50 s wall time. Permission-retirement assertions remain covered, including a real allowlist change after an auth-only config commit.
- Review found older config-event expectations in chat, New Session, and command-palette tests. Those now expect retention; explicit policy-change and connection/identity retirement cases remain intact. All 110 tests in those three files passed (18.65 s wall time including the requested changed-lane dry run).
- The existing operator-model-policy reload regression passed unchanged. The first CI run caught the obsolete UI expectations (UI shard: 230.38 s); they were corrected rather than rerun unchanged.
- Catalog-mode coverage now verifies unrestricted merge-to-replace retirement while metadata is held. The added assertion failed before the comparison fix; all 65 lifecycle/web/terminal tests passed afterward (32.58 s). A built Gateway `config.patch` smoke observed `modelSelectionChanged: true` on that transition.
- No real provider inference or paid API calls were made. This PR addresses retention of existing choices, not immediate publication of new provider rows.

Before (blocking state; dark theme):

![Open picker replaced by Loading models during sign-in](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/41fae691-3234-40f9-98fa-22c83ebf667e)

After (existing provider choices remain available; light theme):

![Open picker retains existing choices while discovery refreshes](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7f0000f6-6161-40f4-83fd-b7f148945da7)

fix: model pickers ignore clicks during startup loading (#158128)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes model pickers ignoring clicks after opening the Control UI on a freshly started Gateway, even when model rows are already known.

## User Impact

The chat model chip opens while history loads. Settings lets users browse known primary-model choices while configuration loads; choosing a different default still requires configuration readiness and mutation access. Sending, active runs, disconnection, and model-switching guards remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Chat history readiness should not control model browsing. Settings likewise separates opening a list from permission to change the default. This changes no configuration or protocol.

## Evidence

A built baseline and candidate ran against an isolated Gateway with synthetic provider models:

- Baseline: the chip displayed the known model but remained `aria-disabled=true`; a click at 1.79 seconds was ignored. Candidate: the first captured click opened the picker in 103 ms while history was still loading.
- Baseline Settings: known rows arrived at 1.43 seconds, but the trigger waited until 1.67 seconds for configuration. Candidate: the trigger enabled 11 ms after the model snapshot, before configuration arrived, and opened successfully.
- Settings regression suite: 36 tests passed (6.39 seconds wall); disabled options still reject changes while shared config work is pending or mutation access is absent.
- The 19 Settings E2E cases pass after updating the old trigger-disabled assertions to exercise browsing while blocked options reject mutations (41.93 seconds wall). Existing state and authorization guards are retained. No full local suite was run.

fix(ui): show failed goal outcome checks (#158021)

## What Problem This Solves

Refs #157961. A saved Goal mutation can reach the Control UI's **Check outcome** recovery control after an unconfirmed ACK. If the idempotent replay fails without a definitive Gateway rejection (for example, `UNAVAILABLE`), `runGoalOperation` retained the saved receipt but explicitly cleared `chatError`. The user saw the same recovery banner with no explanation after clicking.

This change shows the unknown-outcome guidance together with the concrete Gateway error. The original operation identity remains saved; the UI does not infer success from the current goal, invent a new mutation, or replay a chat turn. A definitive rejection still follows its existing retirement behavior. The reported already-settled server operation lacks a captured failing RPC response, so this PR addresses the source-proven *silent failure* path; it does not assert a cause or automatic dismissal for that separate observation.

## Evidence

- **Isolated real-Gateway rendered proof (2026-09-25, head `aa7e2fd`):** A temporary browser harness launched a real Gateway on isolated state/port with a synthetic owner, active Goal, and unused fixture model provider. The rendered **Pause goal** control sent the real `sessions.goal.update`; Gateway responded `{ok:true,replayed:false}`. The browser WebSocket route withheld only that ACK. After the browser timeout, the rendered **Check outcome** control replayed **identical params and operation ID**; Gateway responded `{ok:true,replayed:true}`. The route then substituted synthetic `UNAVAILABLE` only on the return path. The patched UI displayed `Goal update not confirmed. Check its outcome before making another change. Synthetic receipt transport interrupted` and kept **Check outcome** enabled. `pnpm test:ui:e2e ui/src/e2e/goal-157961-real-proof.e2e.test.ts` — **1/1 passed**, 191.23 s command duration (8.179 s case). [Inspected after screenshot](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Olli0103/openclaw/evidence/goal-157961-20260925/after.png), [sanitized observations](https://github.com/Olli0103/openclaw/blob/evidence/goal-157961-20260925/after.json), and [reproduction harness/limitations](https://github.com/Olli0103/openclaw/tree/evidence/goal-157961-20260925). The harness was removed from the PR worktree after capture. This proves real Gateway replay plus controlled browser receipt failure, **not** a real network outage or the cause of the separate already-settled-operation observation.
- **Rendered before comparison (old source branch, mock Gateway):** Temporarily restored the exact old catch (`setChatError(host, rejected ? formatUiError(error) : null)`) and ran the same committed browser regression scenario through the rendered **Check outcome** button with `UNAVAILABLE`. The selected case asserted `.chat-error` was absent and captured an [inspected before screenshot](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Olli0103/openclaw/evidence/goal-157961-20260925/before-mock.png): `pnpm test:ui:e2e ui/src/e2e/chat-goal-recovery.e2e.test.ts -t 'shows a failed Check outcome'` — **1/1 selected case passed**, 17.86 s command duration (1.241 s case). Source and test were restored clean after capture. This comparison uses a **mock Gateway**, not an identical real-Gateway before fixture: real-Gateway counterfactual attempts lost the banner after Gateway session-change refresh before the follow-up click and are not presented as successful proof.
- **Source before/after assertion:** At the named non-definitive `runGoalOperation` catch, the old source called `setChatError(host, null)`; the new source emits the unknown-outcome guidance plus `formatUiError(error)`. The committed rendered regression asserts the new visible error after the same **Check outcome** action and would fail against the old catch.
- **Rendered Control UI regression:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts --configLoader runner ui/src/e2e/chat-goal-recovery.e2e.test.ts` — **6/6 passed**, 29.21 s command wall time; new browser case 1.246 s test time. The new case starts Resume through the rendered button, withholds its ACK, reloads, clicks the rendered **Check outcome** button, verifies the replay uses identical request params/operation ID, rejects it with `UNAVAILABLE`, and observes the Gateway error text on screen. The control remains available, no `chat.send` occurs, and another reload restores the saved recovery without sending a request automatically. fix(agents): delivered turns get the channel formatting rules once (#158028)

Related: #157877
Related: #108264

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a turn delivered to Telegram gets the channel's formatting rules in a different shape, twice, or not at all, depending on how it started.

- Reply turns carry the rules inside the inbound metadata. On an account with `richMessages: true`, they also get a separate "Collapsible Details" section, so the `<details>` rule arrives twice.
- Cron announce turns (#157877) carry the same rules in a second block with a different schema.
- Subagent and requester announce turns, and other delivered agent turns (inter-session steps, `openclaw agent --deliver`), get no formatting rules.

## User Impact

User impact: every turn whose visible output is delivered to a channel gets that channel's formatting rules once, in one block. This covers replies, heartbeats, cron announces and subagent announces. For Telegram, the rich-message rules apply only when the delivering account has `richMessages: true`. Other accounts get the standard-formatting rules. Turns with no chat delivery get no rules: no delivery, webhook delivery, subagent children, and Control UI chat. Slack announces now get Slack's rules too. No config change is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

- One core function builds the block: `buildDeliveryFormatPrompt`. Reply turns read the loaded plugin that received the message, as before. Cron and agent-command turns resolve the delivering plugin with on-demand loading, for example for the first cron announce after startup. It asks the plugin for the delivering account's rules and renders one trusted `### Delivery Format` block (`openclaw.delivery_format.v1`) into the extra system prompt. This is the path every runtime (embedded, Codex, CLI) and its compaction already reads.
- Three entry points call this function, each only when its turn has a channel delivery target:
  - Reply metadata, which also covers heartbeats and system events.
  - Cron delivery resolution.
  - Agent-command session preparation, for turns that deliver or use message-tool delivery. It uses the outbound channel and account chosen by delivery preflight, so a turn that starts on one account and delivers through another gets the delivering account's rules.
- Removed:
  - The cron-only builder and its `openclaw.delivery_meta.v1` schema.
  - The `response_format` field in the inbound metadata.
  - Telegram's `markdownDetails` capability. The Telegram contract already contains the `<details>` rule.
- The block has no per-turn fields, so its bytes are the same for every turn kind on the same channel and contract. It stays in trusted system metadata and never enters the transcript. The CLI session-binding inputs are unchanged: replies still keep this block out of the static binding text, and cron still hashes it.
- External ACP agents do not receive OpenClaw's extra system prompt, so they do not get this block. The docs say "OpenClaw agent turn" for that reason.
- Upgrade: the old cron `Delivery Context` block (#157877) is not in any release. Reply turns keep this block out of the CLI session-binding text, as before. A CLI-backed cron session on `main` whose bound prompt text changes resumes with `system-prompt` content drift, not a reset (covered by `src/agents/cli-session.test.ts`, "resumes on content drift").
- Plugin SDK: `inboundFormattingHints` is a shipped field, so this change keeps its name and signature. It is an intentional scope extension: core now calls it for every OpenClaw agent turn whose delivery target is the channel, not only inbound replies. The hook only receives `cfg` and `accountId`, with no inbound message data, so an existing hook returns the same rules it returns today. The SDK docs and type comment describe the new scope.
- Control UI keeps its core-owned `markdownDetails` capability, because it has no channel plugin.
- Follow-ups, not in this PR:
  - A `message` tool send to a different channel than the turn's own still gets only the current channel's rules.
  - `/btw` side answers do not get the block yet.

## Evidence

- Focused tests at the real entry points, with a Telegram stub whose rich and plain accounts return different contracts:
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply.delivery-format.test.ts`: `getReplyFromConfig` replies on a rich account and on a plain account each get exactly one block with their own contract. A Telegram heartbeat through `runHeartbeatOnce` gets exactly one block. A Control UI reply gets none.
  - `src/commands/agent.delivery-format.test.ts`: `agentCommandFromIngress` with `deliver: true` (rich account) and with message-tool delivery (plain account) each append exactly one block after the caller's prompt. A turn from the rich account that delivers through the plain account gets the plain rules. An undelivered turn keeps the caller's prompt unchanged.
  - `src/cron/isolated-agent/run.delivery-formatting.test.ts`: cron announces load the Telegram plugin on demand, as on a cold Gateway. They get exactly one block for rich and plain accounts, and none with `mode: "none"`.
  - `extensions/telegram/src/channel-actions.contract.test.ts`: in the real Telegram plugin, a rich account and a plain account on the same bot get different contracts, and neither advertises `markdownDetails`.
- The tests fail with the old production code restored: both delivered agent-command cases get no block, and the Telegram test finds `markdownDetails`. With the source account used instead of the outbound account, the cross-account case fails.
- Test cost with `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`: about 7.5 s of test time for the agent-command file, 9 s for the reply and heartbeat file, and 4.3 s for the cron file. Most of the wall time is cold transform.
- Neighboring suites pass: inbound metadata, prompt session context, reply media-only, agent command, session preparation and the system prompt. Changed-file typecheck, format and line-cap checks pass.
- Live Telegram Test Server run with a real user recorder and a recording mock provider, on `main` and on this branch (reply and cron code as in the current head):

  | Run | Model request system prompt | Telegram result |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `main`, reply, rich on | rules inside inbound metadata `response_format`, plus a separate `## Collapsible Details` section (the `<details>` rule twice) | rich message |
  | `main`, cron announce, rich on | rules in `### Delivery Context` (`openclaw.delivery_meta.v1`) | rich message |
  | this branch, reply, rich on | one `### Delivery Format` block (`openclaw.delivery_format.v1`, `markdown_telegram_rich`), `<details>` rule once, no `Collapsible Details` section, no `response_format` in inbound metadata | rich message |
  | this branch, cron announce, rich on | the same `### Delivery Format` block, byte for byte; no `Delivery Context` block | rich message |
  | this branch, reply, rich off | one `### Delivery Format` block with the "Telegram rich OFF" rules | plain text message |

  The mock reply is fixed, so the Telegram message does not change between `main` and this branch. No screenshots are attached for that reason.
- Not live-tested: subagent announces, heartbeats, and the Codex and CLI runtimes. They read the same extra-system-prompt input that the focused tests cover.

fix: restore native session browsing with OpenCode v2 (#158056)

Closes #158009

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes empty native OpenCode session catalogs and failed transcript/activity reads after upgrading the OpenCode CLI to v2.

## User Impact

OpenCode sessions remain browsable with either CLI generation, and failed CLI calls now leave a useful Gateway warning instead of only a generic catalog error. No configuration or stored-data migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Detect the installed CLI major version. Keep the v1 database/export commands; use v2's global session API, session export, and bounded event-head probe. Normalize the v2 transcript at the plugin boundary so browsing and upstream human-turn detection share the same interpretation. V2 calls use a private standalone server, an empty temporary config directory, and disabled project configuration; the restricted subprocess environment remains in place.

V2 listing follows API cursors in batches of at least 100 until it has enough unarchived sessions. The complete scan shares the existing 30-second CLI budget and reports an error if exhausted, rather than returning a false empty catalog.

## Evidence

- Real OpenCode 2.0.16, installed from the official `@opencode/cli` package in an isolated prefix: baseline Gateway `sessions.catalog.list` returned no sessions and `LOCAL_READ_FAILED`; the invoked CLI rejected `--pure` and `--format`. The candidate lists both locally seeded sessions, and `sessions.catalog.read` returns the seeded user text.
- Real installed OpenCode 1.18.32 with isolated data: the same Gateway catalog RPC lists the seeded session before and after the change. Neither global CLI installation nor user OpenCode data was changed; no model inference was used.
- Real v2 activity probe: baseline marker established, one external user turn detected, unchanged cursor suppressed, and a confirmed missing session distinguished from read failure. This supplemental probe invokes the plugin activity owner directly; catalog listing and reading above use the actual Gateway RPC.
- Gateway logs now show `OpenCode catalog CLI failed: Error: Session not found: ses_missing158009` for a failed v2 transcript read.
- Focused catalog and activity suites: 37 tests passed, 30.97 seconds wall time including worker preparation. The v2 catalog regression fails against the unchanged baseline with `OpenCode exited with code 2`.
- V1/v2 transcript, activity cursor, transient failure, and missing-session coverage. Broader checks are left to CI.
- Archived-first real v2 store: two recently archived sessions precede one live session. With `limitPerHost: 1`, the earlier candidate returned an empty Gateway catalog; the repaired candidate follows the API cursor and returns the live session. The archived-first regression also fails before the repair and passes afterward.
- Archived-heavy real v2 fixture: 100 archived sessions precede one live session. The actual Gateway `sessions.catalog.list` request with `limitPerHost: 1` returned the live session in 2,430 ms. The regression also verifies that exhausting the shared scan deadline produces an error rather than an empty catalog.

fix(progress): failed commands crowd out plans during active drafts (#156649)

## What Problem This Solves

With tool progress enabled, repeated failed command or tool items took protected capacity in the bounded progress draft. They crowded out the plan and newer activity, so an active turn looked stuck. #142802 fixed this for command-exit rows, but failed tool `item` rows (shell tools, `automations`, plugin tools) still stayed pinned.

## Why This Change Was Made

`isChannelProgressPriorityLine` and Telegram's preview predicate now treat a failed `item` row with a `toolName` as ordinary activity, so it appears when it happens and scrolls out as newer work arrives. Approval requests, `blocked`/`error` states and unnamed failures keep priority. Alongside a plan, one rolling activity slot stays visible. No tool-name list, new progress-line field or snapshot schema change.

## User Impact

- Telegram and Slack card progress with `toolProgress: true`: failed rows no longer hide the plan and newer activity.
- Quiet progress (`toolProgress: false` or summary presentation), including Slack compact style, is unchanged: those drafts store only approval rows.

fix(agents): MCP server tools disappear when catalog listing takes over 1.5s (#157855)

Related: #137379

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: MCP servers with no `requestTimeoutMs`/`timeout` in config lose all their tools for a run when a cold `tools/list` takes more than 1.5 s.

## User Impact

User impact: slow remote MCP servers (streamable HTTP, OAuth) keep their tools in new sessions and cron runs when their tool listing takes a few seconds. Operators no longer need to set `requestTimeoutMs` on each server to avoid random "tool unavailable" results or `Unknown tool id: mcp:<server>:...` failures.

Tradeoff: a server that never answers `tools/list` and has no timeout config now holds tool setup for a cold session for up to 10 s instead of 1.5 s. Servers are listed in parallel (up to six at once), so several hung servers do not add up. An explicit `requestTimeoutMs` still sets the listing timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

Catalog listing used a hardcoded 1.5 s timeout when the server config had no timeout key. The same server's tool calls use the resolved request timeout (60 s default). So a server could show a normal 60 s timeout and still drop its whole tool surface when its list took 1.7 s.

The 1.5 s cap came from #85063. It keeps a hung server from holding up tool setup at session start, because tool setup waits for the catalog. This PR keeps that bound and raises it to 10 s, which admits cold remote listings. It does not use the full 60 s request timeout, because a hung server would then hold up each cold session for a minute. The docs now state the listing timeout.

Credit to @Baumus for the analysis in #137379 that found the mismatch between the resolved timeout and the list fallback.

## Evidence

- Regression test: a stdio server with no timeout config whose `tools/list` takes 2 s keeps its tool. On `main` it fails with `expected [] to deeply equal [ 'slow_tool' ]`. With this change, all 120 tests in `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts` pass. Test cost: `pnpm test src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` takes 73.4 s wall time (Vitest duration 65.9 s, 120 tests). The new test takes 2.2 s of that, from its 2 s delayed listing. In CI run 36092496041 (`checks-node-changed-compact-large-8`) the file's 120 tests took 14.9 s in total; the new test took 2.2 s.
- Real Gateway agent turn: a local streamable-HTTP MCP server configured with only `url` and `transport` (no `requestTimeoutMs`). A Gateway started from source with the QA mock model and tool search off, then one `POST /v1/responses` turn. The check reads the tools declared in the model request.

  | `tools/list` | Build | Gateway log | MCP tools in model request |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | answers after 3 s | `main` | `MCP tool listing timed out after 1500ms` | `[]` |
  | answers after 3 s | this PR | no warning | `["slowlist__slow_lookup"]` |
  | never answers | `main` | `MCP tool listing timed out after 1500ms` | `[]`, turn completes |
  | never answers | this PR | `MCP tool listing timed out after 10000ms` | `[]`, turn completes |

fix(approvals): let OpenClaw change approvals complete in chat (#157947)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: when an agent asks OpenClaw to change config, restart, or manage plugins/channels/agents, the approval never reaches chats without a native approval card, and `/approve <id>` rejects it. The agent's tool call then blocks until the 10-minute expiry, and users are sent to the Control UI or a terminal to approve a change they asked for in chat.

## User Impact

User impact: every approval an agent needs can be completed in the chat where it was requested.
- Native approval cards (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Matrix, Teams, iMessage, Google Chat) keep owning their chats.
- Every other requesting chat now gets the change summary with **Allow once** / **Deny** buttons where the channel renders them, plus a `/approve <id> allow-once|deny` line.
- `/approve` now resolves OpenClaw change approvals, not only exec and plugin approvals.

No config options, protocol, or schema changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Delegated OpenClaw changes ("system-agent" approvals) already had native cards (#134670). Two gaps remained outside those cards:

- **Request delivery.** The request was created with delivery turned off, so the shared approval forwarder never posted a fallback. The forwarder now has a system-agent strategy that always targets the requesting chat and is suppressed whenever that chat's native card handles the request. It uses the same typed-button payload and resolved/expired messages as exec and plugin approvals. The system-agent owner publishes the outcome of a decision (applied, or denied) once; approval publication only adds expiry and cancellation, so a denial produces one chat update. The fallback answers only the live messaging chat that made the request: terminal and Webchat requests never fall back to the session's saved chat, and expiry is reported once, from the Gateway's recorded expiry rather than a local chat timer, so a change approved just before the deadline and applied after it reports its applied outcome instead of a false expiry.
- **`/approve`.** The command probed only exec and plugin approvals. It now also resolves system-agent approvals through the canonical `approval.resolve`, after confirming the id is in `openclaw.approval.list`. Canonical resolution records a kind mismatch as a deny, so `/approve` confirms the owner first instead of probing. On channels with their own approver settings (Telegram, Discord, Slack, …), the Gateway checks the sender as the reviewer, the same check as native buttons. Everywhere else only a configured owner (`commands.ownerAllowFrom`) can approve an OpenClaw change: `/approve` sends the sender as the reviewer, and the Gateway checks owner custody against the current config inside the approval store's final decision guard. An ordinary command-authorized sender is refused, and an owner removed after sending `/approve` cannot complete the decision.

Unchanged: approval authority stays bound to the requesting run; free-text "yes" never approves; Full Access still auto-applies; Control UI and the apps can still decide.

Agent-facing text now says what happens: for runs from messaging channels, the `openclaw` tool description says the change waits for approval in this chat (buttons or `/approve`). Webchat and terminal runs, which the chat fallback cannot reach, are told to approve in the Control UI or OpenClaw apps. The gateway-only prompt line points to `openclaw` and `/restart` instead of "ask human".

## Evidence

Real Telegram (Test Server userbot, Convex-leased credentials, fresh Gateway, mock provider), restricted `exec` mode, agent asks OpenClaw to `set logging.level "info"`:

| Run | Setup | What the user saw | Tap | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | tester is owner (native cards on) | 🔒 native approval card, no `/approve` text | **Allow Once** | `answerCallbackQuery` + 2× `editMessageText`: "approved. Applying" → "approved and applied"; final reply delivered |
| C | tester is owner, `channels.telegram.execApprovals.enabled: false` | fallback message with change summary, `/approve <id> allow-once\|deny`, and **Allow Once** button | **Allow Once** | message edited to "approved. Applying…", then "approved and applied" posted; Gateway config on disk has `logging.level: "info"`; final reply delivered |

Telegram Web screenshots from the same leased test account (cropped to the conversation):

| | Pending | After **Allow Once** |
|---|---|---|
| Native card (A) | ![Native Telegram approval card with Allow Once and Deny buttons](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5d3de39a-339c-4b7b-80d5-84f5d46cc575) | ![Native card edited to approved and applied, followed by the final reply](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3e993ffe-3f85-4941-9f31-0904719ea608) |
| Fallback message (C) | ![Fallback approval message with change summary, /approve line, and Allow Once and Deny buttons](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ca78d61c-627e-47b0-9505-66fa7162e540) | ![Fallback message resolved: approved and applying, then approved and applied, then the final reply](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fb4b5e28-074b-4f69-bbcb-053398b94c25) |

With no owner configured, the owner-only `openclaw` tool isn't exposed, so no change is proposed (config unchanged). That's the existing design; DM pairing sets the first owner.

qa-channel (no native approval cards), new scenario `system-agent-chat-approval`: the agent's delegated change posts the approval in the requesting conversation. A command-authorized non-owner (`commands.allowFrom` includes them, `ownerAllowFrom` does not) sends `/approve <id> allow-once` and gets "❌ Only the owner can approve OpenClaw changes in this chat."; `logging.level` is unchanged and the approval stays pending. The owner's `/approve <id> allow-once` then resolves it; `logging.level` becomes `info`; exactly one final reply. On `origin/main` the same scenario times out waiting for the approval in the chat.

Tests: `/approve` (resolves a pending OpenClaw change canonically; never submits a canonical decision for an id owned by another kind; on a channel without approver settings, a non-owner and a revoked owner never reach the canonical decision), channel custody (without approver settings only a configured owner holds custody, and only for OpenClaw changes), `approval.resolve` (custody revoked between the request and the final write leaves the approval pending), approval publication (allowed/denied changes leave the chat outcome to the system-agent owner; expired/cancelled are published once), forwarder (requesting chat gets the prompt and outcome without `approvals.*` config; a running native card suppresses it; terminal and Webchat requests never reach the saved session chat; a change applied after the deadline reports its outcome with no false expiry; the recorded expiry is reported once), plus existing gateway approval and system-agent suites. The new owner-custody and single-publisher tests fail with the fix reverted. Shared approval and forwarder fixtures moved to sibling `*.test-support.ts` modules so the test files stay under the line cap. Wall time for the touched suites: `commands-approve` + `approval-publication` + `exec-approval-forwarder` + `system-agent-approval` + `approval` ran in 59.5s across 3 Vitest shards. `pnpm tsgo:core` clean.

fix(agents): preserve canonical DeepSeek Flash fallback handling (#157304)

Closes #157266

## What Problem This Solves

Canonical `deepseek-flash` misses the core DeepSeek V4 fallback when an OpenAI-compatible route has no active provider stream wrapper. Legacy V4 Flash and Pro already receive that fallback.

## User Impact

Canonical Flash receives the same native thinking parameters and non-native replay cleanup as legacy V4 Flash. API, provider, and explicit thinking-format guards remain unchanged. The requested model ID is not rewritten; no configuration migration is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Include canonical Flash in the existing fallback predicate. The DeepSeek plugin already owns catalog-backed `isDeepSeekV4ModelId`, `wrapStreamFn`, and `resolveThinkingProfile`. Those hooks belong to the selected provider; the missing core fallback serves routes without that owner. There is no existing cross-provider capability exposing its identity predicate here. Core must not import the plugin's private `models.ts`, so this bounded fix retains the known duplicate exact-ID list rather than adding a public SDK hook. Consolidating fallback identity with the vendor owner remains a follow-up. The checked-in catalog advertises `deepseek-v4-pro`, not `deepseek-pro`; this patch does not invent another alias.

The test rewrite preserves all nine original behavioral cases and assertions, and exercises them with canonical and prefixed/suffixed canonical Flash as well as legacy Flash. The small follow-up keeps direct string comparisons instead of allocating an array on each predicate call.

## Evidence

### Built Gateway before/after

Ran the supported `pnpm openclaw gateway run` entry point (which built the checkout), then `node openclaw.mjs agent --agent <isolated-agent> --message 'Reply proof-ok' --thinking high --json` against that running Gateway. No `--local`, internal source imports, mocked stream functions, or intercepted fetch were used.

- Before: main ancestor `dda6e1ceda395dbcfb7d22eaf4b4364b18227cd7`.
- After: contributor head `4e83097c526f397084a59710c229e0870101305a`.
- Separate task-owned homes/state, loopback Gateway and provider ports, synthetic credentials, and a scripted OpenAI-compatible endpoint registered as `deepseek` with a base-URL override.
- Plugins were explicitly disabled to exercise the fallback without the bundled provider masking it.
- Four fresh agent sessions per build: canonical Flash, legacy Flash, legacy Pro, and non-V4 `deepseek-chat`. All eight Gateway turns completed successfully with `proof-ok`; the provider recorded all eight exact POST request bodies and returned valid SSE.
- This proves Gateway dispatch, request serialization, real HTTP transport and response parsing, not acceptance by the external DeepSeek service.

Socket-observed request-body excerpts (omitted fields are unchanged request scaffolding):

| Model | Before `thinking` / `reasoning_effort` | After `thinking` / `reasoning_effort` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `deepseek-flash` | absent / absent | `{"type":"enabled"}` / `"high"` |
| `deepseek-v4-flash` | `{"type":"enabled"}` / `"high"` | same |
| `deepseek-v4-pro` | `{"type":"enabled"}` / `"high"` | same |
| `deepseek-chat` (negative control) | absent / absent | absent / absent |

```json
{"before":{"model":"deepseek-flash","stream":true},"after":{"model":"deepseek-flash","stream":true,"thinking":{"type":"enabled"},"reasoning_effort":"high"}}
```

The regression suite additionally checks non-native replay cleanup, Foundry suppression, explicit thinking formats, preservation of other reasoning controls, and OpenRouter detection. The prior contributor's embedded-transport proof also captured native reasoning replay preservation versus non-native stripping; the Gateway proof above strengthens the entry-point coverage without claiming a tool-history Gateway scenario.

### Final-head validation

After merging current main and simplifying the predicate, repeated all four built-Gateway turns on `e61a6b6164bf7fe4fad87154314778dd0902bf43`: canonical/legacy Flash and legacy Pro all emitted enabled/high, while non-V4 `deepseek-chat` still emitted neither field. All four completed with `proof-ok`.

Focused test run on that source: 27 fallback tests, 142 extra-params composition tests, and 19 DeepSeek plugin tests passed (188 total). The three routed shards took 96.74 seconds total; the changed fallback file took 22.08 seconds in Vitest. No project-wide suite or broad formatter/linter was run locally; hosted CI owns the remaining checks.

### Main update

Merged current main into `2557771e3136743d6ad7153a91c4ac9907cdf011` without rebasing contributor commits. Both fix files are byte-for-byte unchanged from the Gateway-proven revision above. Fresh CI on this head supersedes the earlier run blocked by main's architecture and channel test failures.

fix: Side chat cannot answer on claude-cli installs without an API key (#157474)

Closes #141483

## What Problem This Solves

Control UI Side chat fails with `missing-provider-auth` on subscription-backed `claude-cli` installs without a direct provider API key.

## User Impact

Side chat can answer through a tool-free, one-shot CLI process when direct provider authentication is missing. Working direct-provider installations retain read-only tools and image support. CLI image questions return the existing `image-input-unsupported` error. No configuration, public API, or schema changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The automatic utility model normally uses the embedded runner. Reuse the existing CLI side-question owner only when provider credential resolution reports `missing-provider-auth`; other credential failures are not hidden. Carry the selected logical provider/model into CLI admission so permitted restricted operators can use Side chat.

This follows the [recorded maintainer decision](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/157474#issuecomment-5827253713).

## Evidence

Real built Gateway and Control UI, isolated state, synthetic session, and non-default loopback ports; no real Claude login or paid API key was used. **The external Claude executable and OpenAI-compatible provider are scripted boundaries.** Gateway routing, process launch, session snapshot construction, RPC transport, tool execution, image delivery, and UI rendering are real.

- Main `1976a166443`: asking Side chat with a CLI primary and no API key fails; Gateway reports `No API key found for provider "anthropic"` and the UI displays its error.
- Candidate: the same question answers through the stub `claude`. Captured argv includes `--tools ""`, `--disallowedTools mcp__*`, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--no-session-persistence`, and `--max-turns 1`. Its stdin contains the selected-session text and `ROUTE_PROOF_141483` snapshot marker. No resumed session is used.
- CLI image request: RPC rejects with `image-input-unsupported`, without crashing.
- Direct API-key route, before and after: the scripted provider requests the real `read` tool, reads `proof.txt`, and the answer contains `SIDE_CHAT_READ_PROOF`. A separate image question reaches the provider with the image and answers successfully. The same three read-only tools remain available.
- Focused ask + RPC suites: **30 passed**, 42s wall including worker preparation; CLI/auth upgrade regression about 131ms. Removing the logical requester model makes the restricted-operator regression fail; restoring it passes.
- Runtime-only Gateway + Control UI builds completed. Full declaration build was stopped at its 20-minute timeout; not claimed as passing. Main and candidate both report the same existing 62-byte startup CSS budget overage; no UI assets changed here.

fix: show chat model menus without waiting for discovery (#157899)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: opening `/models` or a channel model picker can wait up to five seconds for inventory discovery even when usable models are already known.

Related: #153796.

## User Impact

Chat model menus return the current known choices while discovery continues in the background. Pending providers retain the existing `checking models…` text, and the next open includes newly discovered models. Discovery does not edit an already-sent reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared menu loader requested a writable catalog read, which waits for full inventory acquisition. It now reads the published catalog and lets the existing owner acquire the full inventory in the background. Native readiness and authentication facts still come from the same owner. Typed model selection and explicit refresh retain their existing paths; no configuration, startup, persistence, or protocol changes are required.

Owner approval:

> “chat pickers answer immediately from known rows, fetch in background”
>
> — Ayaan, 2026-09-25, model-picker invariants program

This decision includes the existing SDK menu builders. The previous implementation
already permitted partial results after its five-second acquisition race; awaiting
a builder was not a complete-inventory guarantee. The SDK compatibility guide now
states the published-row and `pendingProviders` contract explicitly.

## Evidence

Built baseline and candidate Gateways used isolated state and a local vLLM endpoint that delayed its model listing by four seconds. Real `chat.send` commands exercised `/models`; `models.list` was sampled alongside them.

| Observation | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First cold `/models` reply after acceptance | 7.493 s | 1.942 s |
| Replies while provider discovery was pending | 5.2–7.5 s | 185–625 ms after the initial replies |
| Later reply lists the newly discovered model | Yes | Yes |
| Catalog-not-ready errors in 80 `models.list` samples | 0 | 0 |

The first end-to-end candidate reply still includes cold session/admission work; this change removes the catalog acquisition wait, not every source of first-reply latency.

Before, this reply excerpt arrived after the acquisition wait; after, it arrived while the HTTP listing was still pending:

```text
- vllm/known-fixture

vllm: checking models…
```

A later candidate reply contained:

```text
- vllm/discovered-fixture
- vllm/known-fixture
```

Typed selection also completed through the Gateway:

```text
Model set to vllm/discovered-fixture for this session only; configured default unchanged.
```

- The held-acquisition regression fails on the original loader because no reply is produced; it passes with the fix and verifies that the next reply includes newly published rows.
- Focused command and recovery suites: 61 tests passed across the scoped runs. After constructing the immutable snapshot fixture correctly, the messaging typecheck and held-acquisition regression passed; the regression took 1.054 s. The full recovery-file single-worker run took 35.11 s including worker-artifact preparation.
- Clean-clone build, targeted formatting, and `git diff --check` passed. No model inference or paid provider calls were used.

### Telegram Test Server

The checkout's Telegram userbot runner exercised the built candidate with a
Convex-leased Test Server bot and user authorization. The first recorded menu was:

```text
Select a provider:

vllm: checking models…
```

Its button showed `vllm (1)`. The next provider menu offered the known model while
the HTTP listing was still pending. Reopening after discovery showed two model
buttons, including `discovered-fixture`.

The first menu arrived 3.951 s after the send receipt, including Telegram ingress
and cold-admission work; it was observed 17 ms after the four-second HTTP listing
started, well before that listing could complete. The later two-model menu
arrived 1.256 s after its send receipt. This proves nonblocking catalog
acquisition, not sub-second end-to-end Telegram startup.

TDLib recorded three new bot messages and zero edits or deletions: discovery did
not modify a previously sent list. Recording completed, the runner released its
credential state, and neither task port remained listening.

fix: plugin reloads lose tool results and strand subagent settlement (#157339)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: removing or disabling a plugin while an agent turn is running loses that turn's tool result, and a background subagent started before the change never settles. Its completion retries about once per second until the Gateway restarts.

## User Impact

User impact: owners can uninstall or disable a plugin mid-conversation, even through the agent's own `plugins` tool. The running turn keeps its tool output, and subagents started before the change deliver their results and finish.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Admitting Gateway:** each Gateway registry owner now links every registry it publishes to itself. A turn's derived agent-runtime registry (`src/agents/runtime-plugins.ts`) is linked to the Gateway whose request admitted the turn. A registry claimed by two owners, or built by a published build without the link, has no owner, and recovery stays strict for it.
- **Tool results:** a run resolves its tool-result middleware once. When the plugin that owns a middleware was removed mid-run, calling it threw `PluginInstanceUnavailableError`, and the harness replaced the whole tool result with "Tool output unavailable due to post-processing error." The runner now drops a handler only when that handler's own plugin instance is retired and the plugin is gone from the current registry of the Gateway that published it. It checks before choosing a path, so a run whose only middleware was removed returns the untouched result exactly like the no-middleware path. It checks again right before each call. A skipped plugin never runs. Every error a handler throws still fails closed, a replaced plugin fails closed, and a handler whose Gateway is closing or unlinked fails closed.
- **Detached task settlement:** a child run, its lifecycle events and its retry timers keep the parent turn's plugin-generation scope. After a plugin reload that scope's registry is retired, and `captureDetachedTaskRuntimeOwner` refused every core settlement ("Detached task runtime owner changed before task settlement."); each retry captured the same stale scope, so it looped. Lookup and settlement of rows that already exist now resolve through the admitting Gateway's current registry, only while that Gateway is open and core owns tasks in both generations. The owner check runs again right before the terminal write. Task creation stays bound to its admitting scope, so a retired generation cannot admit new task work. A closing admitting Gateway, a different live Gateway, or a successor that registers a plugin task runtime is refused with `DetachedTaskRuntimeOwnerRetiredError` before any task write.

## Evidence

**Production trace (before):** an owner asked the agent to uninstall a plugin that owned tool-result middleware. The `plugins` tool succeeded and two hot reloads followed. About 1 s later the log showed `tool result middleware failed for tool_call`, and the model received "Tool output unavailable due to post-processing error." A subagent started before the reload then logged `DetachedTaskRuntimeOwnerRetiredError` about 2,480 times over about 50 minutes, until the Gateway restarted.

**Live Telegram matrix, built `dist` of `c6a7bf3` vs base `b5346d6`.** Each run uses a real Gateway, the Telegram test server with a real QA user, and a mock provider. The DM or forum-topic turn runs `exec`, spawns a subagent (about 20 s of work), then runs a 12 s `exec`. During that exec, the scenario changes a test plugin that owns tool-result middleware by editing config in place, so the Gateway hot-reloads. "Owner-retired lines" counts `DetachedTaskRuntimeOwnerRetiredError` and "settlement deferred" log lines until Gateway shutdown (about 2 minutes later). The task state is read with `openclaw tasks list --json` at 115 s.

| # | Case | base `b5346d6` | this PR `c6a7bf3` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | DM, plugin uninstalled mid-turn (disable, then remove: two hot reloads, as in production) | Reply `TOOL2_LOST(Tool output unavailable due to post-processing error.)`; 512 owner-retired + 252 deferred lines; child task stays `running` | Reply `TOOL2_OK`; child task `succeeded`; 1 owner-retired line (one retried lookup), then no loop |
| 2 | Same, in a forum topic | Same loss and loop (512 + 252); child `running` | `TOOL2_OK` and the child's result posted in the topic; child `succeeded`/`delivered`; 1 owner-retired line |
| 3 | DM, plugin only disabled mid-turn (one hot reload) | not run | `TOOL2_OK`; child `succeeded`/`delivered`; 1 owner-retired line |
| 4 | DM, new task work after the reload: the same turn waits, then `sessions_send`s a follow-up to its finished child | Tool results lost (3 middleware failures, including the `sessions_send` result); follow-up task created | `TOOL2_OK` and the `sessions_send` result intact; the follow-up task (`cli`, `succeeded`) is admitted on the live generation; child `succeeded`/`delivered`; no owner-retired line |
| 5 | DM, middleware plugin replaced (reinstalled) mid-turn | Gateway refuses: `still has active retained work; … replacement not applied`. User sees `TOOL2_OK` and the child result | Same refusal; `TOOL2_OK`; child `succeeded` |
| 6 | DM happy path, no plugin change | not run | `HAPPY_DONE TOOL_OK`, one reply |

Notes:
- **Case 4:** a turn's new task work goes through Gateway admission, which uses the live generation, so no live flow reaches task creation inside a retired scope. The unit test below proves that such creation is rejected before any write.
- **Case 5:** the Gateway will not replace a plugin whose work is still held, so the fail-closed path for a stale handler with a live replacement cannot be reached from a turn. The loader test below covers it.
- **Cases 1 and 5 (DM):** the child's completion message was still `pending` at the 115 s read. Its direct send failed with `Plugin telegram was reloaded or disabled; use its current tools.` This is the separately tracked Telegram send issue #155788, which this PR does not change.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes selected models getting buried when a provider has hundreds of choices, and catalog recommendations losing their order in Models settings and text `/models` pages.

## User Impact

The selected model leads Gateway browse results and Models settings. Chat and New Session keep the Default reset action pinned in its provider group, then place the current model before the other catalog choices. Text `/models` pages put the current model first. Search still checks the whole inventory.

This does not change model admission, permissions, configuration, or stored data. Dedicated channel button menus and cross-session recency tracking are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep provider ranking in the existing catalog-order owner, then promote the resolved current/default selection without changing the remaining catalog rows. Preserve the deliberate Default/inherit affordance from #145112; it is a reset action rather than another ranked model choice. Models settings no longer replaces catalog order with label sorting.

## Evidence

- The post-main owner run passed 110 cases across core catalog, Gateway model-list projection, text commands, shared/chat pickers, and runtime selection/reset behavior. Four 300-row regression groups (including chat with and without Default) fail with the original ordering restored and pass with the fix.
- The text-channel harness checks a 20-row Slack-style first page containing the current and curated models, plus access to the last page. It does not contact Slack.
- The independently built base returned all 300 configured models, but placed the session's current model at index 297 and the default at index 299. Its web picker omitted the current model from the first visible page; typing the synthetic new model's exact ID still found it. The real TUI initially showed models 000–008 at position 1/300.
- The rebuilt candidate puts both the default and the session's current model at index 0 in `models.list`, preserving every other row's sequence. Real-browser chat and New Session keep Default pinned, immediately followed by the current/draft choice. Models settings keeps its selected model first. Exact-ID search still reaches the synthetic new model. The real TUI starts with the default model, followed by models 000–007 at position 1/300.

refactor(usage): capture hosted pricing once per operation (#157838)

Related: #140086

## What Problem This Solves

Makes each usage-cost operation retain one hosted pricing context, preparing usage accounting for catalog updates that can occur while an operation is running.

## User Impact

No user-visible change in this PR. Catalog downloads still require a Gateway restart to activate. Existing recorded costs, configured overrides, local model prices, and tier handling keep their current behavior. There are no configuration, protocol, SDK, or storage changes.

This is the maintainer-requested accounting prerequisite for live catalog publication, not the activation change itself.

## Why This Change Was Made

Usage refresh previously selected its pricing fingerprint and each lazily resolved model price independently. The refresh now captures the hosted pricing context once and uses it for both. Diagnostic readers retain lazy preparation and capture their context when estimation first becomes necessary; subsequent model lookups retain that context.

The ordinary synchronous pricing APIs still use the same resolver and preserve their existing lookup behavior. Fingerprint-only reads do not allocate an unused captured resolver.

## Evidence

- **Built Gateway, base and candidate:** downloaded a synthetic catalog through `openclaw models refresh`, imported two unpriced transcript records through `openclaw doctor --session-sqlite import`, then called the public `sessions.usage.logs` and `sessions.usage` methods. Base `05edd36e12` and current candidate `c95b7d0942e6` both reported individual costs **$1 and $4**, and total cost **$5**. Each ran with separate state, home, configuration, profile, and loopback ports. No provider inference was performed.
- **Mid-operation regression:** after selecting a new pricing context, an existing operation retains the old price for a model it has not looked up yet and retains its fingerprint; a new operation uses the new prices and fingerprint. Replacing the captured lookup with the previous per-lookup selection makes this test fail with **expected 4, received 40**. This is a controlled pricing-publication test, not a claim that this PR activates downloaded catalogs.
- **Focused suites:** 240 tests across 13 pricing, usage-format, usage-reporting, and usage-worker files passed during preparation. The operation regression was then moved into its own usage-pricing suite to avoid growing the existing pricing suite beyond its line cap; that relocated case and focused lint passed. The current head passed the built Gateway parity check again.
- **Measured cost:** the relocated `session-cost-usage-pricing-context.test.ts` regression took **36 ms** on the current head (21.56 s shard including cold transform). The earlier three-file command took 108.00 s; the remaining ten-file command took 101.34 s. [Exact-head CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36095336705), with all 147 jobs completed and no failures.

Documentation is unchanged because the existing restart contract remains in force.

fix(cron): announce runs miss the channel's formatting rules (#157877)

Related: #108264

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: scheduled (cron) runs that announce to a channel get none of that channel's formatting rules. For example, a daily job that posts to a Telegram chat with `richMessages: true` never sees the rich-message contract. The model guesses the markup, so the same job sends a `<table>` on one day and a `<pre>` block on another.

#108264 moved the Telegram rich contract out of the core system prompt and into the channel's inbound formatting hints. Those hints are only built for turns that start from an incoming message (and for heartbeats, which carry their delivery channel in the same context). Isolated cron runs never build them, so they lost the contract.

## User Impact

User impact: a cron job that announces to a channel now gets the same formatting rules as a normal reply on that channel and account. For Telegram, this is the rich contract when `richMessages` is on and the "rich OFF" rules when it is off. Jobs with `delivery.mode: "none"` or a webhook get no channel rules. Inbound replies do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The channel plugin's `inboundFormattingHints` stays the only source of the rule text.
- Cron delivery resolution now also resolves the plugin that will send the output, with the same outbound lookup that delivery uses. This includes a plugin that is loaded on demand for the first announcement after startup. The hints come from that plugin for the delivering account.
- An announce run adds a short trusted `### Delivery Context` block (`openclaw.delivery_meta.v1`) to its extra system prompt. This is the same path that #108264 uses to reach every runtime (embedded, Codex, CLI). The block stays in system metadata, not in the transcript.
- The block only exists when the job requests delivery, the target resolves to a chat, and the plugin has hints. For each job it is the same on every run, so the prompt prefix stays cache-friendly. CLI session binding hashes the same block, so a CLI session and its media-wake continuation keep resuming.

## Evidence

- New `src/cron/isolated-agent/run.delivery-formatting.test.ts` runs the real cron preparation, delivery resolution and executor. The Telegram plugin is not active and is loaded on demand, as on a cold Gateway. Rich ON adds the rich contract for the delivering account, rich OFF adds the OFF rules, and `mode: "none"` adds nothing. The ON and OFF cases fail on `main`. They also fail with a lookup that reads only the active plugin registry.
- Neighboring cron suites pass: message-tool policy and source-delivery guard.
- Cost of the new test file: `pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent/run.delivery-formatting.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` measures about 4.7 s of test time (33 s wall, most of it cold transform).
- Live check on the Telegram Test Server with a real-user recorder: an isolated cron job announces to the test chat with `richMessages: true` and a mock provider that records requests.
  - `main`: the model request has no delivery context and no `markdown_telegram_rich`.
  - This branch (current head): the developer-role system context of the model request contains the `openclaw.delivery_meta.v1` block with `text_markup: "markdown_telegram_rich"` and the full rule list.
  - On both, the Telegram user received the reply as a native rich message with a table block. The mock reply is fixed, so this shows delivery still works. It does not show a change in model behavior.
- Not live-tested: the CLI and Codex runtimes. They get the same extra-system-prompt input as the embedded runtime that was tested.
