fix: recover proxy completions sessions when output budget is exhausted (#157673)

Closes #157307

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes sessions getting stuck without a useful reply when an OpenAI-compatible proxy prompt consumes its configured context budget.

## User Impact

Exhausted thinking-enabled requests enter existing bounded compaction recovery instead of repeatedly sending a one-token output limit. Normal budgets and deliberately short completions that fit remain unchanged. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the insufficient-budget warning with a context-overflow error before provider I/O, using the existing 16-token useful-output floor for reasoning-capable models with thinking not disabled, only when context pressure reduces the requested budget. Non-reasoning and thinking-off requests retain the existing clamping and one-token fallback exactly, including when the estimate leaves zero or negative space. This preserves useful short replies while recovering reasoning-only stalls, using existing model.reasoning metadata and the already-resolved request thinking mode rather than a new heuristic. Any broader estimated-budget policy is outside this fix and remains a separate follow-up. Keep the context cap and the payload-aware clamping introduced by #85889; reuse the diagnostic floor from #140902. Recovery remains owned by the existing runtime, with its existing attempt limits.

Maintainer decision: thinking-enabled requests reduced below the existing 16-token floor enter bounded overflow recovery. The conservative estimate can compact a request the provider tokenizer might have fit; if the prompt cannot be compacted, the turn fails visibly rather than silently looping on one-token reasoning-only replies. Non-reasoning and thinking-off behavior, including the ordinary insufficient-budget warning and one-token fallback, is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Real isolated Gateway against a scripted loopback OpenAI-compatible reasoning provider, configured with contextTokens=16384 and maxTokens=2048, with thinking explicitly enabled for the final red/green. Synthetic history filled the session through normal agent turns.
- Before: normal requests used max_tokens=2048; the next two turns sent six requests with max_tokens=1, received reasoning-only output, and failed without compaction.
- After: the same stored session invoked compaction (summary budgets 1638 and 1024), retried with max_tokens=2048, and returned NORMAL_REPLY. The following turn also returned NORMAL_REPLY at 2048. No one-token request was sent after the fix.
- The fixture initially emitted an invalid compaction summary, correctly rejected by the existing quality guard; after matching its required headings and pending ask, recovery completed without editing session state or changing configuration.
- Regression cases for exhausted and sub-floor thinking-enabled budgets fail against the original producer (3 failures) and pass with the fix. The useful-floor boundary and an intentional one-token request are preserved.
- After merging repaired main, repeated the real Gateway red/green with the narrowed guard: the baseline again sent six one-token requests across two failed turns; the candidate compacted and returned normal 2048-budget replies on recovery and the following turn.
- Non-reasoning Gateway control: the same near-cap prompt returned OK with max_tokens=15 on both baseline and candidate, with no compaction. Focused tests also preserve the 1-token boundary.
- Thinking-disabled Gateway control: a reasoning-capable Qwen-compatible model with --thinking off sent enable_thinking=false, retained max_tokens=15, and returned OK. The existing Qwen reasoning test now exercises a fixed near-cap system prompt with thinking off versus on.
- Focused tests after the final refinement: 20 parameter tests, 20 reasoning-policy tests, and 44 overflow-recovery tests passed (40.57s wall combined after merging repaired main). Full suites were not run locally.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the Gateway logs `SQLite reclamation Worker failed` at warn level when automatic session maintenance is superseded by a session write during planning, which is the expected outcome and retries on its own.

Automatic maintenance intentionally rejects a plan when its inputs change before commit and reschedules after the write quiet window. The Worker diagnostics could not tell that refusal from a crash, so every one logged as a failure.

fix(plugins): updates fail when a plugin dependency assigns to import.meta.url (#157862)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw update` stops with `Update state snapshot failed (exit): Assigning to rvalue (308:4)` when an installed plugin depends on valid JavaScript that assigns to `import.meta.url`. The error names no file, so the user cannot tell which dependency blocks the update.

A real trigger is `@jsquash/png@3.1.1` (`codec/pkg/squoosh_png.js`), reached through a literal dynamic import:

```js
if (import.meta.url === undefined) {
  import.meta.url = 'https://localhost';
}
```

Related: #146993 (added the native scan path), #155394 (earlier `import.meta` inspection fix).

## User Impact

Updates no longer stop for plugins whose dependencies assign to `import.meta` properties, such as `@jsquash/png` and `@jsquash/avif`. If plugin source inspection still cannot parse a file, the updater error now names that file and says the failure happened after the source transform.

Upgrade path: the installed updater runs the snapshot inspection itself. Installs that already run 2026.9.5 or 2026.9.6 keep the old inspection for the update that moves them to this fix, so that one update can still stop on such a plugin. The update troubleshooting page now documents the recovery for that one update: `openclaw plugins disable <id>`, `openclaw update`, then `openclaw plugins enable <id>`. Updates from releases before 2026.9.5 do not run this inspection in the snapshot. All later updates use the fixed inspection.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Plugin source inspection sends JavaScript that uses `import.meta` through the Jiti transform, so Jiti can rewrite reference anchors such as `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.resolve(...)`. Jiti also replaces `import.meta.url` with a string literal on the left side of an assignment. The output is then not valid JavaScript, and the parser rejects it.
- Before the transform, inspection now replaces an `import.meta.*` expression that receives a value (plain or compound assignment, update, destructuring, `for…in`/`for…of` target) with a plain identifier. The transform output is used only to find references and is never executed, so imports, `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` assets and `import.meta.dirname` anchors are still traced as before. The dependency is inspected, not skipped.
- The fix is in the transform path and not in the native fast path. Other syntax can also select the transform (for example `for (key in object)` in the `@jsquash/avif` encoder), so a native-only fix would still fail on that sibling file.
- If the transformed output still cannot be parsed, inspection now throws a `SyntaxError` that names the source file and the stage, and keeps the parser error as `cause`. Callers that already catch `SyntaxError` (candidate rehearsal warnings) keep their behavior.

## Evidence

Real `openclaw update --tag <future tarball> --yes --no-restart --json`, run in a disposable container with a throwaway profile. The profile has one path-loaded plugin that lazily imports `@jsquash/png@3.1.1/encode.js` and `@jsquash/avif@2.1.1/encode.js` (the published packages, unmodified).

| Installed updater | Update target | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (base of this PR) | base + version bump | exit 1: `Update state snapshot failed (exit): Assigning to rvalue (308:4)` |
| this PR | this PR + version bump | exit 0, updated, only the normal advisory for a `plugins.load.paths` plugin |

fix: preserve CLI session context when compacting runtime aliases (#157870)

Closes #157831

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes loss of native CLI conversation context when `/compact` runs on a `claude-cli/<model>` session with a separate compaction model.

## User Impact

Manual compaction keeps the bound Claude CLI session, including when native compaction fails. Unsupported or unacknowledged native compaction reports failure instead of silently compacting a different transcript.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing compatibility owner matched only the canonical model provider, rejecting the registered CLI backend's own provider alias. Accept that alias for the same registered backend in both runtime and setup discovery, while continuing to return its canonical provider. Provider-switch and ambiguous-binding behavior remain unchanged.

This restores the existing native compactor's success/failure path. No second router or binding-clearing exception is needed: native failures already return before context-engine compaction and its transcript-rewrite invalidation. Normal context-engine invalidation remains unchanged.

## Evidence

- Isolated built Gateway, real `chat.send` turns, a scripted `claude` stream-JSON executable, and a local scripted provider; no real Claude/model calls. Before: `/compact` compacted the OpenClaw transcript, reported completion, and the next CLI invocation started a different session without `--resume`, returning `UNKNOWN`. After: native `/compact` receives `--resume` with the established session ID and the next turn returns the remembered codeword.
- Restart control on the merged candidate: after native compaction and a Gateway restart, the next stub invocation has `--resume` with the original session ID and returns the same codeword.
- Negative acknowledgement: the stub exits successfully without a compact acknowledgement; Gateway reports `Compaction failed`, retains native continuity, and the following turn still returns the codeword.
- Normal-provider manual compaction still completes through the context engine. Four existing model-locked Codex compaction controls pass, covering missing/stale bindings and required-preflight fallback. These Codex controls are focused tests, not a live Codex model run.
- Two new alias rows fail before the fix and pass after it, covering runtime registration and setup-only discovery. The four focused suites (`session-runtime-compat`, `cli-backends`, `compact.native-cli`, `commands-compact`) pass; grouped wall time 142.9s including cold transform. The compatibility/backend shard took 16.26s; Codex controls took 97.1s including cold transform.
- Personally inspected sibling Codex `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs:2338-2354`: `thread/compact/start` loads the named thread, validates its provider, then submits `Op::Compact`. An unrelated native CLI transcript cannot be compacted through that endpoint.

Existing native-compaction documentation remains accurate; no configuration, schema, or API change.

refactor(ui): share catalog reads between New Session and model search (#157832)

## What Problem This Solves

New Session and command palette model search independently own catalog request cancellation, refresh subscriptions, and failure state, making their read policies drift as model discovery changes.

## User Impact

No intentional user-visible change: previously fetched New Session choices remain selectable during a background refresh; a truly cold scope does not fabricate choices from configured defaults. Model search remains independent of slower command categories.

## Why This Change Was Made

This consolidation is an explicitly maintainer-requested deliverable for model-picker freshness: establish one web-client catalog read policy, starting with New Session and the command palette, without reversing truthful cold-catalog behavior. The scope intentionally remains behavior-preserving after baseline proof showed the warm picker already works.

A shared reader beside the existing model-catalog store now owns each view's request and subscription lifetime. The existing cache remains the sole display-data owner; connection/scope retirement, Gateway invalidations and model snapshot publications retain their existing semantics. New Session keeps its account-preview and preference-restoration rules, while the palette keeps its independent search-category lifecycle.

This preserves the cold-catalog decision in #119462 and the independent model search behavior in #151022. Baseline browser proof already showed retained rows during a held refresh, so this PR does not claim to fix a warm-picker loading regression.

No config, schema, protocol, Gateway startup, persistent catalog state, or plugin-loading changes. No migration is required.

Follow-ups deliberately outside this PR: migrate chat-state-refresh, chat-command-executor, Agents settings, Automations, Config, Search, model-providers/load, model-providers/catalog-discovery, model-setup/native-model-setup, and chat-metadata-store to the shared reader where their lifetimes fit.

## Evidence

- Built Control UI with the mocked Gateway in Chromium: baseline and candidate retain fetched rows during a held refresh, including desktop/mobile remount revalidation. Both preserve the cold loading state without exposing the configured default as an option.
- Added the standing held-refresh scenario: select a different fetched model without resolving models.list; the selected label changes and the picker remains nonbusy. It passed on the original base and candidate (candidate: 1.31 s scenario), confirming this is behavior-preserving consolidation rather than a new warm-picker fix.
- New Session and palette component coverage: 175 tests passed across nine files (8.67 s Vitest / 10.02 s command wall). Covers independent model results while another category is pending, recovery through another view's publication, invalidation/retry, stale owners, account previews, and preference restoration.
- Replaced two update-notification-count waits with observable model-state waits; no behavior assertion was removed.
- Complete New Session model-catalog and palette-first-open browser files: 19/19 passed against the built candidate (34.40 s Vitest / 36.19 s command wall).
- Initial CI [run 36086860473](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36086860473) identified two PR-owned static issues and unrelated upstream Madge cycles. The static issues and upstream cycles are resolved on the final candidate.
- Static corrections at `06b184e08d2f` remove the palette's now-redundant optional checks/Boolean conversion and reflow the New Session promise chain. Palette and account/metadata lifecycle coverage passed again: 83/83 tests (12.02 s Vitest / 17.95 s command wall).
- Final candidate `dcf448e5e112` includes upstream import-cycle repairs `818b0092d2e` and `af545bf3b6a`. Exact-head [CI run 36093827970](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36093827970) is green, and hosted ClawSweeper review is `ready` with no findings.
- Rebuilt and replayed both browser files after merging those repairs: 19/19 passed (34.43 s Vitest / 36.29 s command wall).

fix(ollama): stop dropping free-form object tool arguments (#157564)

Closes #157039
Supersedes #157435.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: native Ollama tool calls lose free-form object arguments, causing Tool Search dispatch to fail repeatedly.

## User Impact

User impact: free-form tool input survives native Ollama schema conversion, including nested Tool Search arguments. Closed objects and the root object fallback keep their existing behavior. No configuration changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The request normalizer added `properties: {}` to open objects. Keep the repair in the Ollama request producer, preserving explicitly open objects, pattern-based records, and nested objects with implicit additional properties. The extracted inference and recursive normalization logic is unchanged apart from the empty-properties predicate. The Tool Search transport regression now uses the actual `id` plus nested `args` response contract.

## Evidence

### Real Ollama inference through the built Gateway

Tested head `1071871aa7a9105862e381737071cf2eb0774789` against **Ollama 0.34.4, qwen2.5:3b**, in a throwaway CPU-only Docker container (8 CPUs, 8 GiB, loopback-only port). Image digest: `sha256:8262851b2846b87c649eddf3e76beb270c52f4d1bc94559f47efde16b0841551`. A transparent loopback recording proxy forwarded requests and streamed responses unchanged; unlike the fixture below, it generated no model responses. A registered plugin tool recorded its received arguments independently.

Same prompt on both sides:

> Use proof_record exactly once now. Set payload to this JSON object exactly, preserving all keys and values: {"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK","count":7}. After recording it, reply DONE. Do not just describe the tool call.

| Side / attempt | Actual outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Main normalizer / 1 | Gateway timed out at 300.821 s, no tool execution. The upstream model eventually returned populated arguments after the Gateway deadline; this is not counted as a successful turn. |
| Main normalizer / 2 | After setting `num_thread: 8` to match the container CPU quota, real tool call delivered `{"payload":{"count":7,"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}}`; final `DONE`, 192.372 s. |
| Main normalizer / 3 | Same populated tool arguments; final `DONE`, 3.411 s. |
| PR / 1 | Same populated tool arguments; final `DONE`, 3.475 s. |
| PR / 2 | Same populated tool arguments; final `DONE`, 3.250 s. |
| PR / 3 | Same populated tool arguments; final `DONE`, 3.208 s. |

**Scope:** the real model emitted tool calls on both sides. Qwen2.5 3B did **not** reproduce the reporter's empty-argument inference behavior: both successful baseline turns preserved the payload despite the injected empty property map. The candidate's three successful real inference turns establish after-fix compatibility and actual tool execution, not a live red/green reproduction of that model-specific failure. The source/schema regression and deterministic Tool Search red/green comparison below remain separate evidence.

Observed native wire excerpt (description omitted only for brevity):

```json
{
  "before_payload_schema": {"type":"object","additionalProperties":true,"properties":{}},
  "after_payload_schema": {"type":"object","additionalProperties":true},
  "real_after_tool_calls": [
    {"id":"call_7fdun0ne","function":{"name":"proof_record","arguments":{"payload":{"count":7,"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}}}},
    {"id":"call_l5jkfqoy","function":{"name":"proof_record","arguments":{"payload":{"count":7,"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}}}},
    {"id":"call_d2fnvsic","function":{"name":"proof_record","arguments":{"payload":{"count":7,"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}}}}
  ],
  "tool_received_each_time": {"payload":{"count":7,"message":"OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}},
  "gateway_each_after_turn": {"status":"ok","assistantTurns":2,"toolSummary":{"calls":1,"tools":["proof_record"],"failures":0},"final":"DONE"}
}
```

### Deterministic Tool Search regression and closed-object control

A built Gateway was exercised through `node openclaw.mjs agent --agent main --message ... --json`, using isolated state and a loopback native `/api/chat` NDJSON fixture. The baseline used the main normalizer in the otherwise identical candidate checkout, then the candidate normalizer was restored and rebuilt. The fixture records the exact request and models the reporter's schema-sensitive response: it emits empty nested arguments only when the request gained `properties: {}`. This section is deterministic Gateway/transport/tool-dispatch proof, separate from the real inference runs above.

| Scenario | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Main normalizer, Tool Search | Wire `args` schema gained `properties: {}`. Three `tool_call` responses carried `args: {}`; all three failed target-input validation with `command: must have required property 'command'`. Four provider requests, no successful tool execution. The fixture then ended the bounded reproduction. |
| Fixed normalizer, Tool Search | Wire `args` retained `patternProperties: {"^.*$": {}}` with no `properties`. Response `{id: "openclaw:core:exec", args: {command: "printf OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}}` reached the dispatcher; real `exec` returned `OLLAMA_PROOF_OK`, exit code 0. Two provider requests, one successful dispatch, final `OLLAMA_PROOF_COMPLETE`. |
| Closed-object negative control, before and after | A registered plugin tool with `additionalProperties: false`, required string `value`, and declared properties received `{value: "OLLAMA_PROOF_OK"}` in both runs. Serialized schemas were identical; both turns completed in two provider requests. |

Focused command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/tool-schema.runtime.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/tool-schema.transport.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/stream-runtime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: **203 passed**, 16.83 seconds wall including preparation. With the main normalizer restored, the two schema regression files produced **6 failures and 3 passes**: free-form cases failed on injected empty properties, while root fallback, closed-object, and recursive normalization controls passed. The isolated runtime build (`scripts/build-all.mts gatewayWatch`) passed.

The transport fixture makes no claim to test model inference. Its assertions protect the outgoing schema and parsed nested argument contract; the Gateway exercise separately verifies real dispatch and tool execution.

After merging current main for the unrelated build repair, all four Ollama files remained unchanged. At `1071871aa7a9105862e381737071cf2eb0774789`, the focused suite again passed 203 tests (22.96 seconds wall), the built Gateway again completed the Tool Search/exec turn in two provider requests with one successful dispatch, and the runtime build passed.

fix(channels): match non-TTY setup advice to registered flags (#157551)

Closes #157546

## What Problem This Solves

Headless `channels add` suggested `--use-env` even for channels that do not register it, making the suggested retry fail with an unknown-option error.

## Solution and User Impact

Read the selected plugin's declared setup fields through the existing channel metadata resolver. Modern channels without `--use-env` now point to channel-scoped help. Channels declaring that flag, and legacy adapters that register it through the compatibility set, retain their existing advice. No flags, defaults, config, or exit codes change. The CLI documentation describes both modern and legacy registration.

## Observed Proof

Real CLI via `pnpm openclaw channels add ...`, stdin closed (/dev/null), isolated home/state/config, and an unused Gateway port. Baseline origin/main `5048811d368`; candidate `75ba9dc678c71621063b4d817b187ba8710d4c10`.

| Command suffix | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--channel signal` | Suggests `--use-env` (exit 1) | Suggests `openclaw channels add --channel signal --help` (exit 1) |
| Signal's advised retry | `--channel signal --use-env`: OpenClaw does not recognize option "--use-env" (exit 1) | `--channel signal --help`: lists Signal setup flags, including `--http-url` and `--signal-number` (exit 0) |
| `--channel telegram` | Suggests `--use-env` (exit 1) | Same advice (exit 1) |
| `--channel telegram --use-env` | Set these environment variables before using --use-env: TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN. (exit 1) | Same credential validation, not an unknown option (exit 1) |

Focused checks passed: 71 CLI registration tests, 83 channel-add tests, and the new one-test `src/commands/channels.add.notty-advice.test.ts` command-boundary regression. The new test protects the actual emitted recovery command; the registration test covers modern env/non-env and legacy behavior. The complete patch remains two small production changes (+21 net lines), two test files (+105), and a documentation correction; no extra production machinery was needed.

### Test cost

This PR **adds** `src/commands/channels.add.notty-advice.test.ts`. Measured with `pnpm test src/commands/channels.add.notty-advice.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: **26.935 s wall** on macOS, including a cold compiler cache (17.408 s preparation); Vitest reports 24.47 s, and the case 145 ms. Hosted [checks-node-changed-3](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36064741808/job/107853104067) reports **4.33 s Vitest / 5.70 s wrapper**, case 158 ms. Existing CLI suite hosted duration: 0.904 s / 2.54 s wrapper; added case 2 ms. Local combined CLI and channel-add invocation: 30.237 s wall. No project-wide suite was run locally.

### Regression fixture correction

The command test now mocks the actual `src/plugins/bundled-package-channel-metadata` owner and uses a synthetic `fixture-signal` id absent from bundled metadata. With the old mock path this case failed by emitting the generic environment hint; fixing only the mock path made it pass. This proves the fixture drives the emitted advice rather than ambient manifests. Production code is unchanged from the CLI captures above. Latest one-worker run: 8.708 s wall, 6.86 s Vitest, 12 ms case; CLI suite rerun: 71 passed in 1.623 s wall. Latest CI seconds will be recorded when available.

test(cli): Close the fixture gaps deferred from managed-context/1 (#12712)

The audit of #12700 deferred ten fixture and wording gaps in the
managed-context/1 contract. Close them before W0c consumes the fixtures.

- Identity comparisons are exact. Attestation and installation cases
  answer 409 for identifiers that differ only in letter case, and for
  storage IDs and mount roots that only a normalizer would equate. Session
  and operation IDs that differ only in case are different IDs.
- A context change that touches only the directory, the revision or the
  configuration reference is a conflict, under a new and under a reused
  operation.
- New sequences pin that operation reuse is checked after the digest and
  the Workspace part, and that no refusal records, overwrites or forgets
  state.
- More rule cases: operationId bounds, trailing newlines, non-ASCII
  digits, numeric binding fields, non-string identifiers, signs, a
  padding-only token and loose ready records. Attestation now repeats
  every single-field boot case on an attested field, valid and invalid.
- The Java conformance test pins the schema's enums and its record and
  outcome references.
- The design document names the protocol token, drops the PATH_MAX
  analogy, and states which JSON parsers can read the fixtures. It
  records that the Broker cannot yet tell a refused boot from a crash,
  adds an open question on installation retention, and lists a W0c test

* fix(core): fall back to unlimited for an invalid advisorMaxUses

Nothing validates settings.json on the load path, so a hand-edited -1, 1.5 or
"5" reached the Config constructor and threw from it, taking the CLI down at
startup — with advisorModel "off" too. Under `qwen serve` the daemon still
booted but every POST /session failed with an opaque 500 "agent channel closed
during initialize", which gives a Web Shell user no hint which setting is wrong.

Fall back to 0 (unlimited) through an exported isValidAdvisorMaxUses, the way
the neighbouring numeric settings already do, and announce the ignored value as
a settings warning: the user asked for a limit, so the fail-open must not be
silent. tryConsumeAdvisorUse still never sees a fractional or negative cap.

Patch from @wenshao's maintainer verification, which measured the startup
matrix and the serve probe on a real build. Re-verified here RED->GREEN on both
sides: the five invalid-value cases and the three warning cases fail on
e3add752 and pass with it; core Advisor config 13/13, cli settings 213/213,
prettier and eslint --max-warnings 0 clean on all four files.

* refactor(core): reset the Advisor counter in place, like its sibling

`advisorUsage` is the same kind of session-global counter as
`webSearchSessionUsage`, which this file declares `readonly` and documents as
"never reassigned" because a derived Config (`deriveConfig` ->
`Object.create(base)`) must mutate the shared object rather than shadow it with
an own property. The Advisor counter was neither: it was reassigned, in a second
`if (isSessionTransition)` branch about 24 lines above the block that already
handles that condition and already resets the web search budget.

It works today only because `startNewSession` throws on derived Configs, so no
child ever holds an own copy. Make the invariant compiler-enforced rather than
incidental: declare the counter `readonly`, drop the separate branch, and reset
it in place beside the web search budget.

Raised as triage note 2 and agreed with in @wenshao's maintainer verification.
No behaviour change: the existing "resets the Advisor count when a new session
starts" case fails when the in-place reset is removed (checked by mutation), and
core Advisor config stays 13/13 with tsc --build, eslint --max-warnings 0 and
prettier clean.

Feasibility study for using the Bailian (DashScope) Batch API from Qwen Code: why it cannot serve the agent loop (24h window, no streaming, per-request cost math vs prefix cache), the three shapes that do fit (agent-driven fan-out, headless --batch swap, repo CI offline work), the request-level switch needed to keep the 17 side-call purposes on the realtime path, and a blast-radius plan.

Adds docs/verification/batch-api/: four probe scripts (plumbing, tool-call passthrough, cache-hit-in-batch, queue-timing) with a README and pass criteria. Scripts read DASHSCOPE_API_KEY from env only and delete their own uploaded files; they have not been run yet.

* docs(batch-api): add handoff section with next steps and change-point checklists

* feat(cli): add qwen batch command for DashScope Batch API jobs

Adds `qwen batch submit|status|fetch|cancel` so many independent single-turn requests can be run through the DashScope Batch API at half the realtime price. Credentials resolve the same way as the interactive CLI and only OpenAI-compatible key auth is accepted; the command talks to /files and /batches with native fetch, so no new dependency. The agent loop is untouched — this is the fan-out shape from the feasibility study, not a swap of the main request path.

Not run locally: vitest and typecheck are left to CI per repo convention; the command has not been exercised against the live API yet.

* feat(core,cli): add headless --batch mode routing main turns through the Batch API

Adds an experimental `--batch` flag for non-interactive runs (-p, positional prompt, or piped stdin; rejected with -i or in the TUI). When set, the main loop marks its own generateContentStream request with `executionMode: 'batch'` and the OpenAI pipeline sends that one request through files → batches → poll → output file instead of the realtime route, then replays the finished completion as a single stream chunk so tool-call parsing and the rest of the chunk path are unchanged. Side calls (compression, titles, classifiers, judges) never carry the marker, so they stay realtime; Qwen OAuth is refused because that endpoint has no Batch API. Aborting cancels the batch server-side; uploaded and produced files are deleted afterwards; the batch id is written to stderr so a run that dies mid-wait can be recovered with `qwen batch fetch`.

Not in this cut: batch_id persistence / resume across processes, explicit enable_thinking, cost accounting. Not run locally (vitest/typecheck are CI's per repo convention) and not yet exercised against the live API — the tool-passthrough probe in docs/verification/batch-api is the acceptance test.

* fix(cli): list batch in bootstrap help and prettier-format the batch docs

The bootstrap help table must name every top-level command registered in config.ts (cli.test.ts guards it); add batch there and to the guard's mapping. Also run prettier over the feasibility doc and the probe scripts, which the earlier commits had only lint-checked for TypeScript files.

* fix(cli,core): make `qwen batch` and `--batch` actually run

Three defects the unit tests could not see, all found by driving the real
CLI process against a fake DashScope server (added here as
docs/verification/batch-api/).

1. `--batch` never ran at all. `client.files.create` throws "The provided
   fetch function does not support file uploads with the current global
   FormData class" before a request leaves the process: every Node run
   installs a custom fetch on the client (undici's, pinned to the
   timeout-free dispatcher in runtimeFetchOptions.ts), and the SDK's
   multipart probe rejects any such client. Upload through the global
   fetch instead — the same route `qwen batch submit` already takes.

2. `batch` was missing from the subcommand exit list in parseArguments, so
   a handler fell through to the main flow: every subcommand exited 1 with
   "No input provided via stdin" (a TTY would have entered the UI), and the
   memory relaunch below re-parsed argv in the child, running the handler a
   second time — `qwen batch submit` created two batch jobs and billed
   both, returning only the second id.

3. A settled-but-failed batch reported `Batch <id> failed` and nothing
   else: the reason lives in the error file, which the cleanup then
   deleted. Read it before throwing.

Verified with docs/verification/batch-api/regression.sh (26 assertions,
no network): one batch per submit, exit 0 for all four subcommands,
--batch through a two-hop tool call, the provider's reason on failure,
refusal to fetch an unsettled batch, and SIGINT cancelling server-side.

* test(cli): stop the `batch` exit-list case from running the real handler

Mock ../commands/batch.js the way this file already mocks

Clear process.exitCode in a finally block, matching the neighbouring

* fix(core): delete the batch input file when batches.create fails

`fileIds` and the try/finally both began after `client.batches.create`
returned, so a create failure left the already-uploaded -- and already
billed -- input file on the server with nothing left to delete it. This
change exists to stop leaving billed orphan artifacts behind, so move the
try up one statement and let the finally cover create as well.

`batch` is now declared outside the try as possibly-undefined: the catch has
to tell "create threw" (no batch to cancel) from "polling threw", and
reading a try-scoped `let` from the catch would throw and mask the original
error.

(no maxRetries, no proxy / QWEN_TLS_INSECURE dispatcher, no SDK default or
user customHeaders, no typed APIError with retry-after handling) and that
staying line for line consistent with the `qwen batch submit` uploader in
packages/cli/src/commands/batch.ts is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.

* fix(core): keep --batch out of derived configs (F4)

The sandbox verification measured two remote jobs for one `qwen -p "say hi"
--batch` run, and the second one is the memory-extraction subagent: it runs
on a config built by `deriveConfig`, which is prototype-delegated, so
`getBatchMode()` reached it from the parent. Every subagent and scoped
context inherited it the same way — each paying its own >=24h window and
queue wait for work the user never asked to defer, and contradicting the
feature's own claim that only the main loop's turn is marked.

A derived config is never the main loop, so `deriveConfig` now pins
`getBatchMode()` to false; an explicit override in `DerivedConfigOverrides`
still wins, for a caller that some day wants a batched subagent.

Measured on the fake server, same command before and after: 2 batch jobs ->
1 batch job + 1 realtime call. Pinned by a unit test and by regression.sh's
new R8 (30 assertions, all passing).

* fix(core): stop a failed poll from creating a second batch job (F3)

A transient error while polling propagated straight out of
runBatchCompletion. The caller's retryWithBackoff retries transport errors
and 429/5xx, and a retry of this function uploads a new input file and
creates a SECOND batch — while the first keeps running, billing, and
unreachable. The `finally` also deleted the still-running job's input file
on the way out.

Poll failures are now absorbed (five consecutive ones before giving up), and
giving up throws a plain error the outer retry will not act on, naming the
job and `qwen batch fetch <id>` to recover it. An abandoned job keeps its
files; an aborted one is still cancelled and cleaned up as before.

Driven end to end, not inferred: the harness's new `unpollable` scenario
fails every status poll, and R9 asserts one job created (not two), the input
file kept, and the recovery hint on stderr. 34 assertions passing.

* fix(core,cli): make the batch give-up non-retryable by type, and gate --batch on DashScope

Two findings from triage on bbf79d1.

Blocking: the "outer retry will not act on it" invariant was a comment. The
give-up messages interpolate provider-authored detail, and this repo's
classifier reads provider payloads out of message TEXT — getErrorCode parses
the first {...}, getErrorStatus matches HTTP_STATUS/ddd, isStatuslessThrottle
sniffs for rate-limit bodies. Measured against the real classifier: a give-up
message carrying a rate_limit_error body, or an HTTP_STATUS/503, classifies
as RETRYABLE. A retry re-enters runBatchCompletion and creates a second paid
job while the first keeps running, unreachable — failure mode #4 verbatim,
and throttling is the expected transient failure across a multi-hour poll.
Every give-up now throws BatchNotRetryableError, and shouldRetryOnError fails
fast on its identity rather than on its text. Three tests pin it, including
one that asserts the plain-Error form WOULD be retried, so the guard cannot
rot into a no-op assertion.

--batch is also now gated on an OpenAI-compatible key at a DashScope endpoint.
executionMode is read by the OpenAI pipeline alone — the Responses, Anthropic,
Gemini and Vertex generators ignore it — so the flag used to be a silent
no-op on those: the run went realtime at full price while the user believed
it was deferred and discounted. Reuses the existing isDashScopeProvider
predicate (study §8.3's fail-fast layer), with loopback allowed for a local
proxy and for the regression harness.

Regression: 34 passed / 0 failed. Unit: 2366 across the touched suites.

* fix(cli,core): make the batch gates follow the resolved wire, and stop destroying paid results

Five review findings, each one a path where `--batch` or `qwen batch` did
something other than what its own guard claimed:

- The `--batch` startup gate tested the *selected* auth type while `Config` is
  built with the *resolved* one. A model pinned to `wireApi: "responses"`
  resolves an `openai` startup to `openai-responses`, whose generator ignores
  `executionMode`, so the gate waved through the exact silent full-price no-op
  it exists to prevent. It now tests the value the runtime dispatches on, in
  both directions.
- The "non-interactive only" guard tested the raw variadic positional, and the
  normalizer below drops an empty join — so `qwen --batch ''` on a TTY started
  the TUI with batch mode on, and the first turn typed there became a >=24h
  paid job. The guard now trims what the normalizer keeps.
- The batch upload handed the raw `customHeaders` map to the global fetch,
  bypassing the session-aware wrapper that expands `${session_id}` per request
  and *deletes* an entry it cannot resolve. Literal placeholder text went on
  the wire and the fail-closed drop did not apply. The upload now resolves
  headers the way every other request path does.
- A job that settled without completing had its `output_file_id` registered for
  cleanup and then deleted by the `finally`, destroying lines the user had
  already paid for (`expired`, or `failed` after partial progress) — with no
  recovery path in the error. Those files are now kept and stderr names
  `qwen batch fetch <id>`.
- `qwen batch` dropped the `--proxy` flag (the highest-priority proxy source
  everywhere else in the CLI) and `--insecure`, because this command path exits
  before `loadCliConfig` runs. Both are threaded now.

Also, from the same read: `qwen batch` refused on the selected auth type but
then dropped the resolver's effective one, so a responses-wire model uploaded a
body the provider rejects per line; a create that failed ambiguously (5xx, or
an unreadable body after acceptance) deleted the input file of a job that may
exist and be billing; a download cut short left a truncated file under the
exact name a complete one has; a `custom_id` written on a bare body was lost as
the identifier *and* sent to the provider as an unknown field; duplicate ids
made the output rows unmappable; an envelope line with no `body` had its
declared method/url silently rewritten to the defaults; a UTF-16LE input file
(the PowerShell 5.1 `>` default the BOM comment names) failed with a message
that did not name the cause; and a job reporting no `expires_at` — observed
null on a live endpoint — had no upper bound on the wait at all.

Every fix carries a test, and each test was mutation-checked: reverting the
fixed line alone turns exactly its own test red (9 mutants run).

* docs(batch): record the live measurements, and stop the harness from certifying falsely

The shipped docs still described a pre-measurement world: `batch.md` declared
the two facts that decide `--batch`'s worth "Not measured yet" although both
were measured against the live API a day before that sentence landed (probe 01
passed — tools, tool_calls and an assistant+tool history all pass through a
batch body; probe 02 found `cached_tokens: 0` on both batch arms against a
0.647 realtime control, i.e. `cost_vs_realtime` 1.03). The page now states the
measured result, the latency (596 s for 3 lines, 3718 s for 1000), and what it
means: `--batch` is a switch for a run you leave going, sparing the realtime
quota at roughly realtime cost — not a discount. The auth paragraph now says
what the gates actually check (the resolved wire, and where the two entry
points differ on the host), and the feasibility study's handoff section records
the results instead of listing them as pending.

In the probe harness:

- `submit()` re-sent the non-idempotent `POST /batches` under the SDK's default
  two retries, so one transient provider error could create up to two extra
  live 24h jobs whose ids were never recorded. It now passes `maxRetries: 0`,
  as the production path does, and only deletes the orphaned input file on a
  definite 4xx.
- `collect()` labelled every output-file row `ok` without reading
  `response.status_code`, and the provider writes a failed request into the
  *output* file with `request_counts.failed: 0` — so `00-plumbing`'s pass gate
  (and the decision matrix that consumes it) reported PASS for a batch in
  which all three requests failed. `collect()` now splits rows into
  `ok`/`failed`, the gate checks both, and `02-cache` summarises the unfiltered
  rows so its own completeness gate keeps working.
- `02-cache` wrote its resume file only after *both* paid submits resolved, so
  a failure of the second arm discarded the first arm's already-created batch
  id, and the documented rerun bought that arm a second time — contaminating
  the cache-isolation measurement the probe exists to make. Each id is now
  persisted the moment its own submit resolves, and a resume submits only the
  arm whose id is missing.

* fix(cli,docs): enforce the documented submit ceilings, and correct the fan-out cost claim

R2-54: submitBatch named the provider's 500 MB / 50 000-line ceiling as its
design constraint and enforced none of it, and forwarded --window verbatim.
A 50 001-line file or a 12h window was refused only after the whole file had
been uploaded — the billable half of the mistake. All four limits the shipped
doc states are now checked locally: window format and 24h..14d range before
the file is opened at all, then per-line, request-count and total-byte
ceilings inside the streaming loop, each naming the offending line.

The user doc claimed fan-out is half price with the cache-hit rate at 0, and
presented that row under a heading that says the table was measured. Only the
agent-loop row was measured; the fan-out row is derived, and its h = 0 holds
only when the requests share nothing. Most real fan-out shares a system
prompt, and the realtime side caches it: a 500-token instruction over
2 000-token documents saves ~40%, while a 5 000-token few-shot preamble over
500-token items costs MORE than realtime. The table now marks source per row
and a new section gives the 62.5% prefix-share rule, both worked examples, and
how to read h off a single realtime call before committing to a job.

Also folds #12297's harness back in: the two PRs were coupled (its
regression.sh assumes a CLI with no --batch), so splitting them only bought
a smaller diff at the cost of merge ordering and CI blind spots.

Verified: harness 20/20 against the fake server, cli suites 493 passed,
prettier + eslint clean.

still running — left the suite green.

Anchor each case on the phase column instead (`'\tfailed\texpires'`) and assert
neither `running` nor `queued` appears. Mutation-checked: replacing the branch
condition with `false` now turns this test red, where before it did not.

* feat(cli): add agent-prepared Batch API workflow

/batch --api lets the agent prepare a bulk task as a small plan file
(shared rules + source/target items), and the new qwen batch
run/collect/retry/list subcommands assemble the requests, submit them,
track the job on disk, and deliver validated results as files. The
workflow persists submit intent before upload so a lost create answer
is reconciled instead of resubmitted, holds delivery on source changes
or target conflicts, retries only failed items, and keeps Batch usage
out of the interactive session's realtime cache statistics.

* fix(cli): harden batch auto-collect, task lock and collect after review

Four independent reviews (money safety, integration/types/platform,
docs/skill consistency, test tracing) of the auto-collect commit:

Auto-collect
- A submission that cannot be reconciled is announced once ("may exist
  and be billing — check with qwen batch collect") and then no longer
  polled, instead of paging the provider's batch list every 5 min forever.
  A task locked by another process (e.g. a run still submitting) is not
  mistaken for a lost submission.
- No usable Batch credentials: said once, retried every 5 min, never
  latched off for the session. The endpoint is resolved per pass, and a
  task pinned to another endpoint/key resumes when the session switches
  back.
- Notify mode dedups by batch id, so a later retry is announced; it also
  refuses a wrong endpoint/key before querying the provider.
- Tasks run from a subdirectory of the session root are collected.
- resolveEndpoint takes the session's loaded settings and a warn sink:
  no settings re-read from disk mid-session, no stderr drawn over the TUI.

Collect
- One batch failing to collect no longer hides what the others delivered:
  every attempt is tried, the summary rides on the thrown error, and the
  CLI still exits 1.
- A completed batch whose result file is not published yet stays
  awaiting instead of failing every item (which invited a paid retry).
- A batch that create already returns as failed is reported at once.

Task lock
- An empty/unparseable lock (created but not yet written) counts as held;
  only a well-formed lock from this host with a dead pid is taken over.
- Release removes the lock only if it still holds this acquisition's
  token. CLI commands wait up to 15 s for a lock (an open session's
  auto-collector holds it briefly); the message says so.
- Task-file rename retries briefly on Windows EPERM/EBUSY.

Paths: isInsideRoot via path.relative (roots ending in a separator,
`..name` files, other drives); win32 compares case-insensitively; the
no-hard-link delivery fallback holds on EEXIST instead of throwing.

Skill/docs: plan-field errors are the single exception to "report and
stop"; id length; `collect later with` is only the manual fallback;
latency figures reconciled; dangling section references and an internal
billing detail removed; stage B uses notify mode so auto-collect does not
skew timing; `list` help text. Tests for each fix above.

fix(cli): notify when the Linux clipboard tool is found but its query fails (#12666)

* fix(cli): notify when the Linux clipboard tool is found but its query fails

On Linux, getLinuxClipboardTool() only probes `command -v wl-paste/xclip`; it never touches the display server. With a stale or dead X server (or a compositor socket that went away) the probe passes while the actual query — xclip -t TARGETS -o or wl-paste --list-types — fails, and the paste was swallowed silently: non-zero exit, spawn error/throw and timeout all collapsed into a bare false, indistinguishable from "no image".

Thread onUnavailable into checkClipboardForImage() and getWlPasteImageTypes() and invoke it at each failure exit (non-zero exit, spawn error, spawn throw, timeout), so the caller's unavailability warning fires. A successful query that finds no image still never notifies, so copying text stays quiet, and the no-tool path is unchanged.

Refs #12505 (finding 1 of 3).

* fix(cli): keep an empty Linux clipboard from claiming the native module is broken

Linux clipboard tools use one non-zero exit code for both "the display
server is dead" and "nothing is on the clipboard", so keying the
unavailability notification on the exit code made the image-paste binding
report that the native clipboard module could not be loaded whenever the
clipboard was simply empty.

Capture fd 2 in checkClipboardForImage() and getWlPasteImageTypes(), the
same way saveFromCommand() already does so a non-zero exit can be
diagnosed rather than merely reported, and skip the notification when
stderr identifies the exit as a benign empty clipboard:

- xclip: "There is no owner for the ... selection" (xcprint.c
  errconvsel(), exit(EXIT_FAILURE) when XGetSelectionOwner() is None)
- wl-paste 2.x: "Nothing is copied" (bail() is fprintf(stderr) + exit(1))
- wl-paste 1.x: "No selection" (same bail() path)

An unclassified non-zero exit still notifies, and the spawn-throw,
spawn-error and timeout notifications are left untouched.

* fix(cli): clear the painted text selection when its controller unmounts

The highlight range is painted onto the per-stdout frame controller, which
lives outside React, so it outlived the controller that painted it: ink
re-reads it on every serialization pass and stamps the background onto
whatever cells now occupy those coordinates. A selection made in a teammate
transcript therefore survived the tab switch and was re-stamped over rows of

eventsPaused, which exists to keep the selection that the open context menu's

the effect is stable and its cleanup runs exactly once, on unmount.

main -> teammate, and agent -> agent (AgentChatView keys its boundary on
agentId) all unmount the surface that owns the selection.

On POSIX the bin launcher now runs the CLI in-process and exposes gc at
runtime, so --expose-gc is no longer in process.execArgv. The supervised
relaunch built its child's flags from execArgv alone, so the session
process lost global.gc in --acp, stream-json, --json-fd, file input,

* fix(cli): relaunch when env files injected values

#12602 re-boots a one-shot run whenever .env or settings.env injected
values, because modules that read the environment at load time (and
Node itself, e.g. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS) only see them in a fresh image.
The in-process path ran ahead of that check and skipped it for both
interactive and -p. Take the in-process path only when no env-file
value was injected; otherwise relaunch as main does.

The Bun standalone flavor (the OpenTUI preview archives) runs the same

* feat(cli): Declare the v2 execute/status/cancel Managed Runtime contract

Extend the owned managed-runtime route manifest with the three tool
operations and add their shared schema and conformance fixtures. The
wire shape fixes the evidence rules the recovery design demands: every
call is keyed by the original reference (sessionId, promptId, callId,
argsDigest) rather than any Broker-side identifier; status is read-only
and answers unknown with 200 instead of 404 or 500, because a missing
record is never evidence that a call did not run; a settled state is
the only one that may carry a result; and status additionally returns
the Runtime's own lastSequence cursor. Execute accepts up to 256 KiB
of request input, and every operation answers at most 1 MiB.

No handler is mounted yet: per the manifest rule the routes join in the
same line of slices as the execute extraction that implements them. The
TypeScript gate test proves the owned-route gate admits exactly these
paths, and the Java consumer pins the route contract, every outcome
classification, and the closed field sets, so the worker and transport
slices that follow share one reviewed target.

Related to #12380.

* fix(runtime-broker): Accept unknown cancellation status

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* feat(cli): Mount the v2 tool operations on the Managed Runtime worker

The attestation worker now serves execute, status, and cancel beside
attest. Its executor admits exactly the first-slice ordinary tools —
read_file, write_file, edit, and foreground run_shell_command — over a
real Config rooted at the attested workspace cwd, with checkpointing
disabled and no further approval gate, because admission happened on the
Harness side. An in-memory journal answers status and cancel by the
original reference; it is process-local by construction, since the worker
process is the Runtime generation and a restart is a new generation
rather than a continuation.

execute is idempotent by reference.callId: the same identity joins the
in-flight invocation or returns its settled result, and the same callId
with a different digest or payload is a 409 identity conflict. status is
read-only and answers unknown with 200 for a reference the Runtime never
saw. cancel settles a prepared invocation without touching the tool,
aborts an executing one, and a cancel the Runtime honored settles as
cancelled whether the tool surfaces the abort as an error or as an early
result. The worker's HTTP requestTimeout is disabled because an execute
call holds its connection until settlement.

Related to #12380.

* refactor(core): drop the reviewed-declaration tombstone, gate on the record

The tombstone existed so the review map could be pruned on removal without
opening the never-reviewed pass-through. It did not hold: the record loop
fingerprinted only tools hidden at render time, so a tool reviewed while
revealed kept no entry, its removal wrote no tombstone, and a replacement
publishing a changed contract was invoked with arguments the model wrote
against the schema it actually saw.

Remove the pruning rather than complete it. A retained entry can only match
the same server, schema name and parameter schema, so it either still
describes the live tool or forces a re-review, and no removal route has to
remember to touch the map. Record every tool tool_search returns, not only
the hidden ones, so reveal state no longer decides gate coverage.

(the reveal-state hole); moots R4-1, R4-5 and R4-6, which were all
properties of the tombstone. Design doc updated in both languages.

test(java): wait for a renewal at the advanced time in lease renewal tests (#12656)

* test(java): wait for a renewal at the advanced time in lease renewal tests

dispatchLeaseIsRenewedUntilExecutionCompletes and
provisioningLeaseIsRenewedUntilProvisionerCompletes waited for "any new
version" after advancing the mutable clock. A renewal that landed on the
real-time scheduler just before the advance satisfied that wait, so the
lease still ended before the second advance and the test failed with
"Runtime provisioning claim expired" (seen on macOS CI for #12655).

Wait instead for a lease that ends after the next advance, which only a
renewal made at the advanced time can produce.

* test(java): make the lease renewal waits exact and diagnosable

The post-advance wait accepted any lease end past "advanced time + 40 ms",
which only rejects a stale pre-advance renewal while the fixture lease is
between 40 and 80 ms. From 81 ms up the stale renewal satisfied it and the
tests passed without proving a renewal after the advance.

Both tests now share advanceAndAwaitRenewal: it reads the current lease
end, advances the clock by one step, and waits for the lease end to equal
the old end plus that step, which only a renewal stamped after the advance
produces. Each wait names what it was waiting for, and the post-advance
wait reports the observed and expected lease end.

feat(cli): list managed Agent View sessions in qwen sessions ps (#10942)

* feat(cli): list managed Agent View sessions in qwen sessions ps

`packages/cli/src/agent-view/` is 11,004 production lines with no
consumer: the supervisor, the PTY workers and the session lifecycle all
merged (#7799, #7800, #7801/#9986), while the two PRs that would give
them an entry point are still open (#7802 commands, #7803 roster TUI,
both since 2026-07-27). Nothing calls the subsystem, so nothing that
subsystem knows can reach a user.

This gives it its first one, at the smallest surface that carries real
information: `qwen sessions ps` now lists managed sessions beside the
interactive ones it always listed.

The command walked only the live-process registry, which a supervisor's
worker never writes — so a background session waiting for an answer was
invisible to every listing. `managed-rows.ts` merges both sources into
one row shape, deduplicating by session id (a managed worker can also
register, and would otherwise be listed twice: once as `interactive`,
once with its real state). Managed rows come first, because a session
waiting on input is the usual reason to run this.

Three decisions worth naming:

- Rows are labelled by task state, not by the roster's display group.
  The group folds `ready`, `stopped` and `failed` into one `completed`
  bucket, which the roster UI can afford because it also paints an icon
  tone; a one-line table has no second channel, and printing "completed"
  beside a session that failed is a lie the user cannot see through.
- The name comes from `deriveAgentViewPresentation`, so this listing and
  the roster cannot drift into describing one session two ways. Its
  `Untitled session` placeholder is the single override — the roster can
  afford identical rows because a user arrows onto one; here the session
  id is the only thing that tells two apart. The placeholder is now
  exported rather than duplicated as a literal.
- A supervisor store that cannot be read degrades to the registry half
  and says so on stderr. Silently omitting a session that needs input is
  the failure this command exists to prevent, and stderr keeps `--json`
  stdout parseable.

The table gains a STATE column; `--json` gains a `managed` discriminator
on both row kinds, and carries each registry record through verbatim
rather than looking it back up by session id — two records can share one
(a stale writer, a restored transcript), which would emit one twice and
drop the other.

* fix(cli): hold managed session rows to the registry's identity standard

Both blockers on this listing are the same mistake in two places: the
merge joins two sources that disagree about what identifies a session,
and each half trusted its own spelling.

Pids. `liveWorkerPid` gated durable recorded pids with a bare
`isPidAlive`, and the worker file recorded no process identity at all.
Nothing reaps that file while no supervisor runs — `clearAgentViewWorkerPids`
does not get to run after a SIGKILL or a reboot — so once the OS recycles
the number, `kill(pid, 0)` answers "alive" about an unrelated process and
`qwen sessions ps` prints it next to a row still reading `working`; a
script reading `--json` kills a stranger. A `~/.qwen` shared between
machines or namespaces (an NFS home, a devcontainer with the home
mounted) needs no recycling to reach the same place. The interactive rows
in the very same table are verified with `isSameProcess` plus namespace
and boot-id guards, so the two halves answered to different evidence
standards.

The supervisor now records the start token for each pid it writes, plus
its own PID namespace, and the reader checks `isSameProcess` against
them. All three fields are optional: `AgentViewWorkerFile` is a durable
`schemaVersion: 1` record, and a file written before they existed carries
none, which `isSameProcess` reads as "no identity recorded" and degrades
to exactly the liveness check this command did before. The namespace
guard fires only on a known disagreement, so an unreadable `/proc` on
either side never blanks a real worker's pid.

Ids. `mergeSessionRows` deduped with a case-sensitive `Set.has`, but the
supervisor store reports the sanitized, lowercased directory name it
files a session under while the registry keeps the raw spelling the
worker registered with — adoption keeps both on purpose, because the
native session store is case-sensitive. A managed session whose id
contains an uppercase letter therefore slipped the filter and listed
twice, once with its real state and once as `interactive`, with `--json`
emitting two different spellings for one session. Both sides now
canonicalize through `sanitizeSessionId`.

That sanitizer moved from `supervisor-store` to `protocol`, which is
where it belongs — it defines the identity two readers must agree on, not
a detail of writing files — and it keeps the pure row module free of a
dependency on the filesystem store. `supervisor-store` re-exports it, so
no caller changes.

Tests pin the two arms liveness cannot see: a live pid whose recorded
token no longer matches, and a foreign-namespace worker file. Two more
pin the degradations, since silently blanking every pre-identity pid
would be the worse regression. The mock mirrors the real `isSameProcess`
contract rather than stubbing a verdict, so the existing dead-pid cases
still exercise the fall-through they were written for.

Typecheck, lint and tests were not run locally; CI is the authority on
this branch.

feat(sdk-java): Reconcile and adopt restored Runtime bindings (#12627)

* feat(sdk-java): Reconcile and adopt restored Runtime bindings

A persisted READY binding outlives the Broker process that provisioned
it, but until now a restarted Broker could only fail closed with
runtime_reconciliation_required: the lease was in no process's live set.

For bindings whose request carries a durable provisioner kind, the
Broker now persists a recoverable identity (provision seed encrypted at
rest, scheduler resource handle, attestation generation, last reconcile
time), claims the binding, observes the physical resource through the
new provisioner reconcile operation, re-attests the Runtime identity
through the transport, and only then admits sessions. UNKNOWN and
STARTING observations retry inside an operation deadline that fires
independently of loop progress; a timed-out operation releases its
claim, so a late write is fenced by the operation-generation CAS. A
NOT_FOUND observation marks the binding LOST, and an idle LOST slot is
reclaimed into a fresh generation while an active session keeps the
loss pinned. An identity conflict moves the binding to
RECOVERY_BLOCKED, which never transitions on its own.

Legacy (non-durable) provisioners keep the exact previous behavior:
their restored bindings still fail closed, their provisioning lifecycle
is unchanged, and their claims still lapse instead of being released.
LocalProcessRuntimeProvisioner keeps reporting the legacy kind until a
later slice teaches it ready-record adoption.

Related to #12380.

* fix(sdk-java): Release rejected durable runtimes

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(sdk-java): Block recovery on attestation conflicts

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(sdk-java): Release sessions from lost runtimes

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(sdk-java): Keep ensured resources and guard reconcile single-flight

- Persist the scheduler resource handle before provisioning so a
  retryable failure after ensureResource keeps the binding in
  PROVISIONING and the retry converges on the same resource instead
  of minting a replacement Runtime over an orphaned one.
- Wrap startReconciliation in safeStage so a synchronous claim failure
  removes the published single-flight future instead of hanging every
  later warm/acquire for the binding.

* fix(sdk-java): Bound provisioning and harden durable recovery identity

Durable provisioning now runs under the same operation deadline as
reconciliation, so a parked ensureResource, provision, or attestation call
releases the claim instead of holding the binding open forever, and LOST
reclamation is single-flighted on the binding key with reconciliation so
concurrent warms observe one new generation instead of one spurious
unavailable failure.

requireLiveBinding reads the live-binding map once again, so a concurrent
invalidate cannot turn the domain error into a bare NullPointerException.

The provision seed now also binds the runtime instance of the lease, the
resource handle compares by its canonical encoding so a JSON round trip stays
equal, and the JDBC update no longer re-encrypts the immutable seed on every
renewal tick. Encryption contexts derive from a fixed-width digest of the
binding id so a legal 512-character identifier fits the bound the protector
enforces, the reconciliation backoff can reach its documented 2s cap, the tool
execution table gains the index its binding query needs, and the
provisioner_kind columns match the identifier limit the Java API accepts.

* docs(design): Sync broker docs with durable recovery behavior

The core service design still described the pre-recovery world: an absolute
FAILED write, an unconditional runtime_reconciliation_required, a plaintext
token column, and restart adoption as a non-goal. Split each claim into its
legacy and durable cases, document the encrypted seed and the SecretProtector
key responsibility, add LOST and RECOVERY_BLOCKED to the state model as active
non-terminal states, and scope the reconcile-before-reuse duty of the embedding
service to bindings without durable identity.

* fix(sdk-java): Wait out transient attestation failures and free wedged sessions

Recovery blocked a restored binding on any non-retryable attestation error,
but the transport reports a throttled or incompatible route (429, 408, 404,
a malformed response) as a non-retryable incompatibility too. Only a failure
that is evidence about identity now blocks; anything else leaves the binding
READY so a later attempt adopts it once the transient condition passes,
instead of wedging the row behind an operator.

A Broker killed mid-acquire or mid-release left its Session ACQUIRING or
RELEASING. Both pin a LOST generation, and neither can ever be confirmed by a
Runtime that is proven gone, so the slot stayed wedged with no public API able
to move it. Local settlement now covers any still-active same-generation
session, and a session already RELEASING is settled without another state
transition. A session whose binding is not LOST still fails closed.

Also gives the two retry-count assertions in the recovery tests a 100 ms
operation lease: at 20 ms the deadline (four leases) sat only 30 ms clear of
the 50 ms first backoff, which a loaded macOS runner did not always make.

* docs(design): Correct text that merging main made inaccurate

Adoption re-registers the live binding, so the stale-route guard in the
execution lookup can fail on this base; its comment claimed it could not.

The service core doc still said that a generation which can no longer answer
never blocks its scope. That held only while FAILED was the end of the story:
a LOST generation stays active, so an UNKNOWN execution on one wedges the
scope, and the doc now says so in both languages.

The follow-up list pointed execution-level UNKNOWN reconciliation at #12380,
but reconcileExecution shipped in #12655. What remains is the LOST case.

* docs(design): Cover every unsettled execution in the LOST wedge

The description of a wedged scope named only an UNKNOWN execution, but a crash
leaves the row EXECUTING: nothing moves it to UNKNOWN without a same-key
retry, a cancel or a takeover scan, reconcileExecution answers IN_FLIGHT for
it, and both active-execution queries still count it because they exclude only
SETTLED. Whichever rule eventually settles these has to cover EXECUTING and
DISPATCHING as well, so both documents now say so.

* fix(cli): keep one-shot system-reminder prefixes out of shell mode

Fixes #11626.

Two gaps let `<system-reminder>` text reach bash or misroute queued
input around shell mode:

- handleFinalSubmit prepended the recovered-agents and the
  worktree-restore one-shot notices even in shell mode, where the
  leading `<system-reminder>` is a bash syntax error — and consuming
  the one-shot latch there dropped the notice before any model turn
  could see it. Both notices are now gated on `!shellModeActive` and
  stay armed for the next model-bound prompt. (The workflow-keyword
  reminder was already shell-gated.)
- The queue drain routed submissions on the live shell-mode flag at
  drain time, so a flip while an entry waited in the queue could send
  a shell command to the model or a model prompt to bash. Shell intent
  is now recorded at submit time (addMessage/restoreMessages), travels
  with the queued entry, and the drain/submitQuery route on
  `shellModeIntent ?? shellModeActive`; batches stay intent-homogeneous
  so one routing decision never misroutes another entry. Producers
  that record no intent keep routing on the live flag, as before.

hooks/use-llm-stream.test.tsx, hooks/useMessageQueue.test.ts — the new
cases are red on the unfixed source (prefix reached shell-mode

* fix(cli): batch queued submissions by the head's intent run

popNextSubmission selected every queue entry matching the first plain
entry's recorded shell intent, so a later same-intent entry overtook an
earlier different-intent one. Queueing a model prompt, a shell command
and a second model prompt while a turn was responding drained both
prompts as one batch and left the command queued behind them: the model
answered the second prompt against the pre-command tree, and the command
then ran with no prompt consuming its output.

Take the contiguous same-intent run from the head instead. That keeps
per-entry routing and submission order together; the only cost is one
extra model turn when a shell command sits between two prompts, which no
longer merge. batch[0] is still plainMessages[0], so the batch turnKey
and the key peekNextUserBatchKey reserves for the Goal runtime are
unchanged.

The case that pinned the old reorder now asserts order preservation, and
a new case pins that adjacent same-intent entries still aggregate.

feat(cli): Declare the v2 execute/status/cancel Managed Runtime contract (#12630)

* feat(cli): Declare the v2 execute/status/cancel Managed Runtime contract

Extend the owned managed-runtime route manifest with the three tool
operations and add their shared schema and conformance fixtures. The
wire shape fixes the evidence rules the recovery design demands: every
call is keyed by the original reference (sessionId, promptId, callId,
argsDigest) rather than any Broker-side identifier; status is read-only
and answers unknown with 200 instead of 404 or 500, because a missing
record is never evidence that a call did not run; a settled state is
the only one that may carry a result; and status additionally returns
the Runtime's own lastSequence cursor. Execute accepts up to 256 KiB
of request input, and every operation answers at most 1 MiB.

No handler is mounted yet: per the manifest rule the routes join in the
same line of slices as the execute extraction that implements them. The
TypeScript gate test proves the owned-route gate admits exactly these
paths, and the Java consumer pins the route contract, every outcome
classification, and the closed field sets, so the worker and transport
slices that follow share one reviewed target.

Related to #12380.

* fix(runtime-broker): Accept unknown cancellation status

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(cli): Enforce the v2 tool contract, admit only attest

The route manifest declares the v2 execute/status/cancel contract, but the
raw gate treated every declaration as admitted, so three unimplemented
operations reached Express ahead of any handler. The gate now admits only the
attestation route it serves, and each handler expands admission in the change
that mounts it.

The shared schema also enforced less than the documented contract: one
permissive request body covered all three routes, and nothing tied result to a
settled state or lastSequence to status. Each route now binds its own closed
request body, every ok case must carry a response body, result outside settled
is rejected, and lastSequence is rejected outside status. Mutation tests break
one rule at a time to prove each constraint is load-bearing, and the Java
conformance test reads the renamed definitions.

Both design doc pairs now separate contract declaration from gate admission.

* studio: whole-model NVFP4 for the video families with hosted pre-quantized denoisers

Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, Wan2.2-T2V-A14B (both experts), HunyuanVideo-1.5 480p and 720p run NVFP4 on the
torchao backend from hosted pre-quantized denoisers, so a load never quantises 5 to 28 GB of dense
weights on the fly. Every admitted linear (min 512 features, in and out divisible by 16) is NVFP4;
nothing is per-layer here.

- one shared auto walk with a per-family head in front of it, and divisible_for_scheme
- ZeroRowSafeLinear, a live bug: torchao's nvfp4 activation path raises on HunyuanVideo-1.5's
  empty image stream on every text-to-video render
- loader gates on the packed-weight fingerprint, the component and require_divisible
- conventional video pre-quant seeding, all components or none, with the memory plan taking the
  artifact's resident size rather than the dense build peak
- registry rows for the four hosted NVFP4 repos

nvfp4 stays an explicit opt-in here; no family gets an auto row on this branch.

The tooling that builds and fingerprints these artifacts is not in this repo. It lives in the
private scripts repo with the rest of the quant generation tooling.

* studio: per-layer NVFP4 image policies, flashinfer FP4 backend and a gated auto row

Whole-model NVFP4 does not pay on the image DiTs. A per-layer policy that puts NVFP4 on the few
linears whose activations tolerate it and keeps fp8 everywhere else does: a memory lever at
fp8-parity quality, not a speed win.

- diffusion_nvfp4_policy.py: exact dotted-suffix rules with expected counts, so a diffusers
  rename breaks the resolution instead of shipping a different model
- the _v3 policy checkpoint format, biconditional with a declared policy, and baked activation
  global scales in place of the running-min calibration that was behind the flux black-frame latch
- diffusion_nvfp4_ops.py / diffusion_nvfp4_linear.py: a flashinfer mm_fp4 backend that re-expresses
  the torchao payload rather than requantising it, with two custom ops so the layer compiles
  fullgraph with no graph breaks
- diffusion_nvfp4_protect.py: per-step W4A16 on the same bytes, opt-in, default off
- the reviewed gate record, the only thing that can put nvfp4 into the auto ladder, and the
  conditional Wan2.2-T2V-A14B row that needs flashinfer to be the selected backend
- diffusion_speed.py: stream-merging DiTs compile regionally with dynamic=False, which is what
  FLUX.1's CantSplit inductor failure needed

The tooling that builds, calibrates and gates these artifacts is not in this repo. It lives in the
private scripts repo with the rest of the quant generation tooling.

* studio: NVFP4 flashinfer backend kernel items (device guard, persistent barrier, bias path, cached dispatch)

Four items on the flashinfer NVFP4 path, all found while measuring it:

- every flashinfer call sits inside a device guard, enforced by a source test, because a missing
  guard has taken cards down on a multi-GPU host
- the one-element barrier between quantiser and GEMM becomes persistent rather than allocated per
  call, which is what makes it capture-safe
- diffusion_nvfp4_bias.py: a Triton bias add with a measured numel floor and ceiling, so the kernel
  only runs where it beat the eager path
- the backend dispatch is resolved once per load and cached, instead of re-probing per layer

Carries the same strip as the branches below it: the quant generation tooling lives in the private
scripts repo, not here.

The residency plan counted every accelerator storage of the old pipeline as

* Studio: install flashinfer on demand for NVFP4 loads

An explicit NVFP4 image or video load (or an nvfp4 prequant seed) now installs
FlashInfer when it is missing, instead of silently falling back to torchao.

- Pins flashinfer-python 0.6.6, the version the dispatch allowlist and the op
  fakes were checked against, plus the flashinfer-jit-cache built for the
  running CUDA (cu128 / cu129 / cu130, newest same-major build not newer than
  the runtime). Without a jit-cache the host must have nvcc, else it refuses.
- Every installed distribution is pinned to its exact version through a
