Studio: read text, Markdown and HTML uploads in the encoding they were written in (#11896)

* Studio: read text, Markdown and HTML uploads in the encoding they were written in

Without a byte-order mark, a .txt, .md or .html upload was decoded as
UTF-8 with errors="replace". A Windows-1252 file, which Notepad and Excel
write in Western Europe, lost every accented letter to U+FFFD, and an HTML
page in Shift_JIS or GBK lost nearly all of its text.

_decode_text() keeps the byte-order marks and reads UTF-8 as before. For
bytes that are not UTF-8 it honours the charset an HTML page declares in
its first 1024 bytes, when that charset writes ASCII as ASCII, and
otherwise reads Windows-1252. A file that is UTF-8 apart from a few
damaged bytes still keeps its text, with U+FFFD for just those bytes.

* Trim comments in RAG text decoding

* Keep universal newlines and decode declared charsets as browsers do

Reading bytes directly dropped the newline translation text-mode open()
did, so CRLF files no longer split on the chunker's paragraph separator.
Map declared labels to the WHATWG superset (iso-8859-1 -> cp1252,
shift_jis -> cp932, gb2312/gbk -> gb18030, ...), and fall back to cp1252
unless valid non-ASCII outweighs replaced bytes, so a stray valid UTF-8
sequence in a cp1252 file no longer garbles the whole file.

* Reuse the web fetch WHATWG charset prescan for RAG HTML uploads

core/inference/tools.py already sniffs <meta> charsets the way browsers
do (comment and attribute aware, full WHATWG label table). Use it instead
of a second, weaker regex and label map. A declared UTF-8 (or UTF-16,
which WHATWG reads as UTF-8) page whose bytes are not UTF-8 falls through
to the same fallback as an undeclared one.

* Honor a UTF-8 byte-order mark before the legacy fallback

A UTF-8 BOM file with one damaged byte failed the strict decode and fell
through to cp1252 (or a conflicting <meta> charset), turning the BOM into
mojibake. Decode it with replacement like the UTF-16/32 BOMs; the BOM is
more authoritative than anything else (WHATWG Encoding, decode).

* Keep UTF-8 when damaged bytes only tie valid non-ASCII

A short UTF-8 file with one truncated or damaged character ("caf\xc3\xa9\xff")
has one valid and one replaced character; requiring valid to outnumber
replaced sent it to cp1252 ("cafÃ©ÿ") where the merge base read "café\ufffd".
Break the tie toward UTF-8; cp1252 text still has far more invalid bytes.

* Read declared ISO-2022-JP HTML instead of its escape sequences

ISO-2022-JP is 7-bit, so its bytes always pass the UTF-8 decode and the
page was indexed as ESC$B... escapes (whose '<' also broke the HTML strip).
When a UTF-8-valid HTML page carries ISO-2022-JP escapes and declares that
charset, decode it as declared.

fix(studio): recover from a dead Metal GPU queue instead of failing every later request (#11383)

* fix(studio): report a dead Metal queue instead of hiding it

Three ways an MLX failure reached the user as "An internal error occurred" with nothing in the log.

`_mlx_optional_fusion` guards entry so no optional fusion can fail a load or a request that worked without it. That guard is right for every entry failure but one: once Apple's watchdog has killed a command buffer, the process's GPU refuses every later submission, so there is no unfused path left to fall back to. Logging "continuing with native inference" and carrying on produced a model that answered at 0.097 tok/s and then failed every request. A dead queue is now re-raised, which fails the load and lets the worker be reaped -- the only way back to a usable queue.

"Dead queue" is deliberately narrow. `mlx/backend/metal/device.cpp` formats every `MTLCommandBufferStatusError` as `[METAL] Command buffer execution failed: {description}`, so `Insufficient Memory` shares the wrapper with a watchdog kill, and mlx clears the error when the next commands are encoded. Packing allocates memory native inference never needs, so an allocation failure there is exactly the entry failure the fallback exists for; matching the wrapper would have refused to load models that run fine unfused. Only the watchdog kill and the post-kill refusal count.

`safe_error_detail` recognised none of this. `[malloc] Unable to allocate` fell through to the generic fallback, and "GPU Timeout Error" matched the connection branch, so a dead GPU was reported to the user as an upstream network problem. The Metal and allocation wordings are now classified, ahead of that branch.

`_friendly_gen_stream_error` logs the cause it is about to replace. All four `except GenStreamErrorRaised` handlers funnel through it and none logged anything, so a local generation failure left no server-side record at all, unlike its `except Exception` neighbours.

* fix(studio): retire an inference worker whose Metal queue has died

Apple's GPU watchdog kills a command buffer that stalls, and every later submission from that process returns SubmissionsIgnored. The process itself stays healthy, so nothing reaps it: a fault raised mid-generation left a live worker that failed every subsequent request with a generic internal error. A failed load was already reaped by load_model, which is why that path recovered on a retry.

The orchestrator now inspects every worker response where it is read -- `_read_resp` for direct reads, the new `_read_mailbox` for dispatcher-routed ones -- rather than where an error is reported. Cancellation consumes a fault and discards it without reporting, and a dead GPU queue makes generation crawl, so stopping is the likeliest way to meet one.

A fault may only retire the worker that produced it. A request's mailbox outlives the process it was opened for, so `_WorkerMailbox` carries that identity rather than sampling the current one; `_read_resp` takes the handle before the queue, leaving the harmless pairing when a reload lands between the two. The teardown and the model-mirror clear run under `_subprocess_shutdown_lock`, the lock load_model publishes under, and the mirrors clear only once the process is confirmed dead -- a child that survives SIGKILL keeps its handle and still holds the model.

kept as frozen weights so it round-trips. Sequences past index_topk train
dense and warn once. import_fixes answers only AutoConfig's "Unrecognized
model" on this config.

Resolve remote-code model classes, reach per-expert submodules with LoRA, run the root dispatch hook on the embedding's device (Nemotron-Labs-Teacher) (#11543)

* Let a remote-code from_pretrained cast a 4-bit model's unquantized floats

microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B overrides from_pretrained and ends it
with model.to(dtype), where dtype falls back to the model's own dtype.
transformers refuses every dtype cast on a bitsandbytes model, so the 4-bit
load stopped with "You cannot cast a bitsandbytes model in a new dtype"
while the 16-bit load was fine.

For the duration of Unsloth's own from_pretrained call, and only when the
model is loaded with trust_remote_code in 4-bit or 8-bit, PreTrainedModel.to
casts the floating tensors that are not packed bitsandbytes weights
(Params4bit with a quant_state, Int8Params with an SCB) and leaves the
packed weights alone. Device moves and unquantized models keep transformers'
own path, and the original method is restored when the load returns.

* Keep padding-free off a forward that cannot take packed_seq_lengths, and let a wrapper inherit gradient checkpointing support

Padding-free batching adds packed_seq_lengths to every batch. A remote-code
forward with a fixed signature (microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B) raised
"got an unexpected keyword argument 'packed_seq_lengths'" on the first step
after the 4-bit load was fixed. Auto padding-free and packing now stay off
when the model's forward, looked through PEFT, accepts neither that key nor
**kwargs; a string model or an unreadable signature leaves the decision as
it was.

nvidia/Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B wraps a complete NemotronHForCausalLM in
a PreTrainedModel that keeps transformers' default
supports_gradient_checkpointing = False, so Trainer's
gradient_checkpointing_enable raised "does not support gradient
checkpointing" although every layer underneath supports it. After the
load, a wrapper that says no while a nested model says yes now says yes on
the instance; transformers enables checkpointing by walking modules, so
every layer is switched on as before.

* Train the language model of a wrapper whose forward cannot take a text batch

nvidia/Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B wraps a complete NemotronHForCausalLM
as language_model behind a forward whose first parameter, pixel_values,
has no default and whose body indexes image_flags. A text-only SFT batch
stopped on the first step with "missing 1 required positional argument:
'pixel_values'" once the load, the LoRA targets and the trainer setup
were fixed.

After the load, a wrapper whose forward requires an input that a text
batch does not carry, with exactly one direct child that is a
PreTrainedModel with its own forward and both embedding accessors
(language_model or thinker when several qualify), hands training to that
child, and the generation-time siblings are dropped so their weights are
freed. Every transformers VLM defaults its image inputs to None and is
returned unchanged, as is anything ambiguous.
UNSLOTH_KEEP_COMPOSED_WRAPPER=1 turns this off.

* Recognise gradient checkpointing support from transformers' checkpointing layer

NemotronHForCausalLM's remote code builds every NemotronHBlock on
transformers' GradientCheckpointingLayer but never sets
supports_gradient_checkpointing on the model class, so Trainer's
gradient_checkpointing_enable raised "NemotronHForCausalLM does not
support gradient checkpointing" once training reached it. A model built
on that layer now counts as supporting it, alongside a nested model that
says so itself.

* Carry the wrapper's loader state onto the core that replaces it

from_pretrained records is_loaded_in_4bit, is_quantized, quantization_method,
hf_quantizer and hf_device_map on the object it returns, not on its children.
PEFT reads is_loaded_in_4bit off the model it is given to pick lora.bnb.Linear4bit
over the plain lora.Linear, so a core returned without the flags trained through
the wrong LoRA layer: the forward ran, but merging wrote a 16-bit delta into
packed 4-bit weights and the fast QLoRA path was skipped. The flags now move to
the core, the device map is re-keyed from the wrapper's names to the core's, and
the wrapper config's quantization_config is carried so a saved core still says
it is 4-bit.

Tests: the carried state on a synthetic wrapper, no state invented when the
wrapper has none, and PEFT dispatching Linear4bit on a real 4-bit core; the last
two fail on the branch before this commit.

* Keep the composed wrapper when the load asked for the multimodal model

Unwrapping a wrapper whose forward requires pixel_values was unconditional, so
a FastVisionModel load of Nemotron-Omni meant for image batches lost its vision
tower at load and trained the text core. The unwrap now runs only when the load
carries text intent: text_only = True, or a model with no vision config. A
multimodal load keeps the wrapper and prints the text_only hint, and the
UNSLOTH_KEEP_COMPOSED_WRAPPER opt-out is unchanged.

The two new test files also get the SPDX line the other tests carry.

Test: text_intent = False returns the wrapper with its vision tower and names
text_only = True; a wrapper that takes a text batch prints nothing.

* Keep an unquantized keyword cast inside the tolerated load, and read the bound forward for the packing gate

_tolerate_dtype_cast_on_quantized_model popped dtype out of kwargs and then, on
an ordinary model, handed the call on without it, so model.to(dtype = ...) made
inside a remote-code from_pretrained was a silent no-op: the model stayed
float32. The pass-through now forwards the call exactly as it arrived.

_forward_accepts_packed_seq_lengths read type(model).forward, which on an
nn.Module is never absent (it falls back to _forward_unimplemented, whose
signature takes no keywords), so a torch.compile'd model, which sets forward on
the instance, was read as a fixed signature and padding-free was switched off
for every compiled model. It now reads the bound forward first, as the merged
_forward_accepts_packing_kwargs does.

Tests: the three cast spellings on an unquantized model inside the context, a
compiled kwargs forward keeps padding-free, and the fixed-signature control.
Three fail on the previous commit.

* Unwrap a remote-code composition only when the caller asks for text training

The gate keyed off the wrapper's vision_config, which an audio-only
composition does not have either, so a multimodal load still lost its
wrapper. Only the caller knows the intent: unwrap on text_only = True and
keep the composition whole otherwise.

* Carry the caller's text intent past the loader's normalisation, and count token_type_ids as text

loader.py turns text_only off for a family without its own text decoder so
the full wrapper loads, and forwarded that normalised value as the intent: a
text_only request for such a model kept a wrapper whose forward needs
pixel_values. The caller's own request now travels separately.

token_type_ids is a standard tokenizer field the Trainer supplies, so a
wrapper that requires it can take a text batch and is not unwrapped.

* Only a field the collator supplies excuses a required forward parameter

A required cache_position, use_cache, past_key_values or return_dict is
not something the Trainer puts in a text batch, so a forward that demands
one without a default cannot take a text batch either.

* Resolve remote-code model classes and reach per-expert submodules with LoRA

A remote config that reuses a native class name (NemotronHConfig on the
Nemotron-H hub checkpoints) resolved to the native model class through the
name-keyed auto mapping, so the attention implementation was chosen from the
flags of a class that is never built. The remote class only carries the old
_supports_flash_attn_2 flag, which transformers 5 no longer dispatches on, and
the load stopped with "does not support Flash Attention 2 yet".

resolve_model_class now returns the class transformers instantiates for a
remote config (auto_map entry plus a config class from transformers_modules),
and flash support is read from the flag the installed transformers dispatches
on.

Routed experts kept as per-expert submodules (mixer.experts.<i>.up_proj) were
silently left frozen on standalone text models: the regex FastModel builds only
reaches a leaf directly under the block, while the same layout inside a
vision-language wrapper matched through the language tag. The nested
alternative is added when the requested MLP leaves exist inside experts and the
regex does not already reach them.

* Give the flash fixtures the flag transformers dispatches on, keep the nested-expert test off a stubbed peft_utils

* Run the root dispatch hook where the input embedding lives

accelerate picks the root execution device as the first member of the set of
devices in the map, so a plan that keeps the embedding off that device sends
every batch there first; the embedding hook then carries input_ids on while
attention_mask and labels stay behind. Modeling code that builds its own mask
on the embedding's device (the transformers 4.4x _update_causal_mask the
Nemotron-H hub checkpoints ship) fails with "Expected all tensors to be on the
same device". Native transformers moves the mask itself, which kept the extra
hop invisible. Aligning the root with the embedding also drops both copies
from every batch.

* Fetch a missing remote modeling module with the load's own hub options

When only the configuration module is materialised, the resolver asked
get_class_from_dynamic_module for the repository's default revision with no
token, cache directory or offline flag, so a load pinned to a revision or a
code_revision could read another revision's flags and local_files_only = True
could reach the network. The loader now passes revision, code_revision, token,
cache_dir and local_files_only through, and a other/repo--module.Class
reference no longer consults a same-named module next to the config, which
belongs to a different repository.

Tests: the fetch receives exactly the load's options; a cross-repository
reference resolves in the other repository. Both fail on the previous commit.

A regex the caller wrote, such as one naming the shared expert alone, is
their scope: widening it attached an adapter to every routed expert in

Studio: Qwen-Image-2.1 RoPE in real arithmetic inside the compiled blocks (#11888)

* Studio: Qwen-Image-2.1 RoPE in real arithmetic inside the compiled blocks

Inductor cannot generate complex arithmetic, so the stock complex RoPE falls back to ATen's complex
multiply with a copy kernel on each side inside every compiled block, and the query/key RMSNorm in
front of it cannot fuse with it.

ATen's CUDA complex multiply rounds as real = fma(a, c, -(b * d)), imag = fma(b, c, a * d), which
torch 2.11+ inductor emits exactly for addcmul. The real form swaps the pairs and does one addcmul over
the head dim, so norm and rotation become one kernel with bit-identical output. Used only while
compiling on CUDA with that lowering (probed from inductor's addcmul lowering); eager calls, older
torch and ROCm keep the complex form. Installed before the regional compile when the diffusers
function and its caller match their AST fingerprints. Kill switch UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_Q21_REAL_ROPE=0.

* Studio: real RoPE tests run in fp16 on cards without native bf16

* Studio: real RoPE follows the card's own complex-multiply fusion

nvcc fuses a different product per architecture (B200: imag = fma(b, c, a * d); A100:
imag = fma(a, d, b * c)). install() multiplies a probe on the device, classifies each half against
the two fused forms (exact in float64 on inputs in [1, 2)) and the compiled form uses the same fusion
per lane; a card matching neither keeps the complex form.

* Studio: real RoPE on torch 2.11 only under emulate_precision_casts

torch 2.11 lowers addcmul to one fma only while emulate_precision_casts is set, which Studio's compiled
tiers do; without it the product is split and the real form would not match the complex kernel. The
traced wrapper reads the flag (dynamo guards on it) and keeps the complex form when it is off.

* Studio: real RoPE test bounds the fused norm's rounding per card

The rotation is exact on every card tested; fused with it, the QK norm's reduction can round a few
elements one ulp differently on A100 and L4. The test now allows that, bounded by what the stock
compile already moves against eager.

* Studio: real RoPE fingerprints hash source, not ast.dump

ast.dump output changes between Python versions; the digest now hashes the source with docstrings,
comments and blank lines removed, so it matches on every Python.

* Studio: real RoPE test bounds the fused norm's ulp at the rotation's input

A one-ulp change in the normed input can move a small rotated output by more than its own ulp; the
rotation keeps each pair's length, so the bound is read off the output pair.

Finish a 16bit load of a static per-tensor fp8 checkpoint (Mistral-Small-4) (#11531)

* Finish a 16bit load of a static per-tensor fp8 checkpoint

With load_in_16bit = True on an fp8 checkpoint the loader asks transformers to
dequantize on load, but transformers only folds weight_scale_inv into weights
it has a converter for. A static per-tensor checkpoint such as
Mistral-Small-4-119B ships its MoE stacks as experts.gate_up_proj with a
sibling experts.gate_up_proj_scale_inv (no .weight suffix), so no converter
matches, the raw fp8 values land in the plain Mistral4Experts module and the
scale is dropped as an unexpected key. The first forward then feeds float8
into torch._grouped_mm and training stops before step 1.

After the load, every fp8 parameter whose module carries no scale of its own
is dequantized from the checkpoint scale (per-tensor, per-expert or block
grid) and replaced with its 16bit value. A converted FP8Linear or FP8Experts
keeps its scale and its fp8 forward and is left alone. A card that is already
at its planned 16bit size while its stacks are still fp8 has no room for the
dequant transient; such a stack is parked on the CPU, dequantized there and
moved back once the rest of the card is at its final size.

Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603 in 16bit on two B200s trains 10 steps, loss 0.73 to
1.10 tracking the fp8 cell step for step, where main stops at the first
forward. Fourteen offline tests cover the scale layouts, the VLM key remap,
the converted-module skip and the out-of-memory deferral.

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Map weight_scale_inv back to its weight, and keep no reference to an fp8 Parameter past the first pass

Two problems in the leftover fp8 dequant pass. A checkpoint key such as
layer.weight_scale_inv had its whole suffix stripped, leaving layer, which
the target lookup read as a parameter of the parent module, so a raw fp8
.weight under the standard scale name was never dequantized and hit the same
first-forward failure the pass exists to prevent. And the OOM fallback that
parks a stack on the CPU to free its device bytes could not free them: the
original Parameter stayed referenced from two bookkeeping lists until the
function returned, so the move back onto the card could OOM a second time.

The scale suffix that starts with .weight now maps to the .weight key, and
the bookkeeping keeps parameter names only.

Tests: a standard weight plus weight_scale_inv pair is dequantized, and a
weakref to the original Parameter is dead by the time the CPU pass runs;
both fail on the branch before this commit.

* Refuse a disk-offloaded fp8 leftover, and clean activation scales only on converted modules

A leftover fp8 tensor on the meta device is disk-offloaded: its hook would
restore the raw fp8 bytes at forward time and the checkpoint scale is gone, so
the pass silently skipping it reproduced the torch._grouped_mm dtype failure
one step later. It now raises FP8LeftoverOffloadedError naming the tensor and
the two ways out (keep the model resident, or load_in_4bit = True).

The stale activation-scale cleanup visited every module the checkpoint named,
including an FP8Linear that kept its own weight and scale, and deleted the
activation scale its fp8 forward reads. Cleanup is now limited to modules whose
weights this pass converted.

Tests: the offloaded case raises with the instruction; a module that kept its
fp8 weight keeps its activation scale while the converted one loses it.

* Unpack E8M0 scales, chunk the per-tensor 3-D path, and return a stack that could not be finished to its device

A uint8 scale is an MXFP8 E8M0 exponent, 2 ** (byte - 127), not a multiplier;
casting the byte applied a scale up to 2 ** 128 too large.

The per-tensor fast path materialised a whole 3-D expert stack in fp32, eight
times its fp8 bytes at once, before the chunk budget could apply, which is
what drove the OOM fallback on the checkpoints this pass exists for. A 3-D
stack with a per-tensor scale now takes the chunked branch.

A stack parked on the CPU by pass 1 whose pass 2 also failed was left there,
turning the dtype error into a device mismatch on the first forward; it goes
back to its planned device.

Tests: a per-tensor 3-D stack is chunked; fails on the previous commit.

* Skip the device OOM test on the probe the spoof cannot reach

test_accelerator_skip_guards flagged this file: the new OOM test gated on
torch.cuda.is_available(), which tests/_zoo_aggressive_cuda_spoof.py
patches to True process-wide. Sharing a pytest session with
tests/version_compat or tests/vllm_compat would un-skip it on a CPU-only
box, and it needs a real card.

has_real_cuda() from tests/_shared is the probe that survives the spoof,
and is what the rest of the suite gates on.

Reverting to the torch probe fails the guard again.

* Keep a dequantized parameter trainable, and clean activation scales per attribute

A full fine-tune loads its parameters trainable; the 16bit replacement froze
them, so the experts silently sat out the run. An expert block whose
gate_up_proj was converted while down_proj kept its own scale lost
down_proj's activation scale too; the cleanup now follows the converted
attribute, and a module-level scale goes only once nothing in the module is
fp8.

* Read a variant's own shard index, and put a parked stack back on a shape failure too

A variant load names its files model.<variant>.safetensors, so the leftover
pass now reads that index instead of skipping the repair and handing back a
model with fp8 experts. A stack parked on the CPU by pass 1 is restored to
its planned device when pass 2 finds the scale does not tile it, the same as
when pass 2 raises.

* Orient a transposed block-scale grid by the configured block size, and treat any out of memory error as one

When both orientations of a block grid tile the weight, the shape alone
cannot tell them apart; the checkpoint's weight_block_size decides. A plain
RuntimeError whose text says out of memory (HIP, XPU, WSL, wrapped CUDA) now
defers to the CPU pass like torch.OutOfMemoryError does.

* Studio: faster MiniMax-H3 video VAE encode and decode

Fused Triton passes for the Diffusers AutoencoderKLMiniMaxH3 path:

- encoder: per-frame GroupNorm + SiLU + reflect/causal pad in one kernel
  writing channels-last, conv biases folded into the next fused pass,
  single-frame encodes convolve only the last temporal tap, float16
  encoder under default/max
- decoder: residual + RMSNorm, QK RMSNorm + partial rope in place and
  SwiGLU fused with the reference rounding points kept; spatial tiles
  batched per decoder call
- decode scope that holds allow_fp16_accumulation off unless planned
  (max tier on consumer GPUs); opt-in int8 ConvRot decoder

Off keeps the stock path; any fused path that fails at runtime falls
back to the stock forward.

* Studio: H3 VAE share the eager pad fallback, test the condition encode and fp32 residual

Route the reflect then causal pad fallback in the encoder through one helper,
reword the ConvRot group comment, and add regression tests for the keyframe /
ref2va encode through vae.encode with the float16 encoder and for the decoder's
float32 residual stream under the decode autocast.

* Studio: one owner for the fp16 accumulation flag, atomic H3 int8 install

The H3 decode scope and the speed layer's load/unload writes now go through a
shared lock in diffusion_speed. A write that lands while a decode holds its own
value is recorded and applied when the decode ends, and a snapshot taken
mid-decode sees the process value, so an overlapping load or unload can no
longer be undone by a stale restore.

The opt-in int8 decoder quantizes every Linear into temporaries before touching
any module, so a failure part way leaves the decoder fully float instead of
partly converted while the lever reports off.

* Studio: H3 VAE int8 row quantiser matches the torch codes, faster fp32 stats

The Triton activation quantiser divided with the approximate fp32 division and
rounded ties away from zero, so up to about 1 in 10000 int8 codes differed by one
from the torch path. It now uses IEEE division and half-to-even rounding and
matches it exactly for float16, bfloat16 and float32 inputs.

GroupNorm statistics on a float32 NCDHW frame (the conv_in output in the
float32 tier) use half the pixel chunk, 8x faster for that kernel on a B200.
Other inputs launch as before.

* Studio: H3 VAE fast path asks the Windows Triton toolchain probe

Studio installs triton-windows, so on a Windows NVIDIA host the fused VAE path
engaged even when Triton's JIT cannot find the MSVC CRT headers, and every
fused forward then failed once before falling back. The gate now asks the same
crt_headers_reachable probe the compile gate uses, cached per process; off
Windows nothing changes.

* Studio: H3 fp16 encoder hands back the stock dtype

diffusers 0.40.0 (the pinned release) casts the pixels in encode() to the
encoder's parameter dtype, which is float16 once the default tier casts the
encoder. The fused encoder and its stock fallback then returned float16 into
the float32 quant_conv, and every keyframe or reference encode (fl2va, ref2va)
failed with an input/bias dtype mismatch. Both now return the dtype the stock
encoder had, so the result is the same as when the pixels arrive in float32.

The regression test casts the pixels the way the pinned release does, so it
fails without the fix whichever diffusers is installed.

An AST check that _load_h3_modular_pipeline engages apply_h3_vae_speedups once,
after the denoiser's speed layer, that no other load does, and that generate
settles a runtime fallback next to the compile fallback.

Uses the real gate, no monkeypatching, so a Mac, CPU-only or ROCm run proves

The kernels are defined inside _kernels() and this module postpones its
annotations, so Triton 3.2 and older looked up "tl.constexpr" in the module
globals and failed every kernel with NameError: tl is not defined. The fused
forwards then fell back to the stock path once each and the opt-in int8 decoder

Dequantize FP8 weights left raw by text_only and offloaded loads (#11841)

* Dequantize fp8 weights left in plain Linears by a text_only FP8 load

unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 lists `model.language_model.layers.N.mlp.gate` in
modules_to_not_convert. transformers' should_convert_module prefix-matches that
entry against `mlp.gate_proj`, so gate_proj stays a plain nn.Linear and its
weight_scale_inv is dropped as an unexpected key.

On a full load the raw fp8 values are cast to bf16 and
_restore_dropped_fp8_scales rescales them (#6200). With text_only=True the key is
renamed (`model.language_model.*` -> `model.*`), and transformers 5 keeps the
checkpoint dtype for renamed keys on pre-quantized loads, so gate_proj keeps a
raw fp8 weight. The restore helper took any fp8 weight for a converted FP8Linear
and skipped it, so the eval forward failed with
`expected mat1 and mat2 to have the same dtype, but got: BFloat16 != Float8_e4m3fn`.

A module holding an fp8 weight without its own weight_scale_inv / weight_scale
is now dequantized into the load dtype (passed from the three loader call sites,
falling back to config dtype, the embedding dtype, then bfloat16). The result is
bit-identical to the unrenamed load. Real FP8Linear / FbgemmFp8Linear modules
still carry their scale and are skipped as before.

* Restore dropped FP8 scales on offloaded layers through accelerate's weights map

When a device map offloads part of an FP8 checkpoint (a text_only
Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 load on a GPU that is partly in use already), the orphaned
gate_proj weights of the offloaded layers are meta placeholders, and the restore
helper skipped them with a warning. The text_only forward then still hit a raw
fp8 weight on those layers (`BFloat16 != Float8_e4m3fn`), and an unrenamed load
ran them unscaled.

For a meta weight, find the store accelerate materializes it from (the
OffloadedWeightsLoader behind the hooks' PrefixedDataset), dequantize a copy of
the stored tensor and write it into the loader's in-memory state_dict, which it
reads before the disk index, then recast the placeholder so accelerate's cast on
materialize keeps the dequantized dtype. Converted fp8 modules that carry their
own scale are now skipped before the offload check, so they no longer inflate
the "offloaded" warning. The in-place scaling is moved into
_apply_fp8_block_scale unchanged.

* Only scale an orphaned FP8 weight that still holds raw fp8 values

_restore_dropped_fp8_scales treated every 16/32-bit weight that has a checkpoint
weight_scale_inv as raw values transformers cast without their scale. That is
true on a plain load, but not once a load-time dequantize has already folded
the scale in: with unslothai/unsloth-zoo#1339 (dequantize fp8 weights that have
no FP8 container) the orphaned mlp.gate_proj of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 was scaled a
second time, leaving it at a relative error of 1.0 against the bf16 weights,
on device and, since the offload restore, on offloaded layers too.

A 16/32-bit weight is now scaled only while every element lies exactly on the
e4m3 or e5m2 grid, which raw widened fp8 values always do and scale-multiplied
values practically never do. The offload path decides from the stored tensor
accelerate materializes. Checking the dtype alone is not enough: an unrenamed
load hands the raw values over as bf16, and that is the case the helper exists
for (#6200).

Tiny qwen3_5 FP8 on transformers 5.17: with #1339, gate_proj goes from 0.9998
back to 0.0267 relative error and the logits match the reference exactly, on
full, text_only and offloaded loads; without it every cell is unchanged. The
fixtures that stood in for raw weights with arbitrary bf16 values now use
fp8-grid values, as a real load produces.

Studio: propagate the Ollama CUDA runtime to llama-server (replacement for #7563) (#11666)

* fix(studio): propagate Ollama CUDA runtime to llama-server

The Linux/WSL prebuilt installer discovers a CUDA runtime under
/usr/local/lib/ollama/cuda_v* and will select a CUDA runtime line from it,
but that directory is private to Ollama and is not on the dynamic linker's
search path. A prebuilt whose only libcudart/libcublas copy lives there
could not load its CUDA backend and silently fell back to CPU.

The launchers now read the build's install marker and put the matching
Ollama CUDA directory last on the child loader path, so it only rescues
hosts with no other copy and never displaces the runtime that qualified
the build. The whisper-server sidecar does the same, including slim
bundles whose CUDA module is hardlinked from a paired llama.cpp install.

Rebuilt from unslothai/unsloth#7563 by Imagineer99, adapted onto current
main.

* fix(studio): never let the Ollama runtime displace a loader-resolved CUDA

The vendored dir joins LD_LIBRARY_PATH, which precedes the loader's cache and
its default dirs however late the entry sits, so appending it last was not
enough: where ldconfig already answers libcudart/libcublas for that major, the
private copy would still take precedence over the runtime that qualified the
build. Yield the dir only while the loader cannot find both, falling back to
the default dirs when no ldconfig can be read.

The rescue direction is unchanged: with neither the cache nor the defaults
providing the pair, the dir is still added.

* fix(studio): count the multiarch dirs when ldconfig cannot be read

The no-ldconfig fallback probed only the generic loader defaults, but Debian
and Ubuntu glibc searches the architecture-specific /lib/<triple> and
/usr/lib/<triple> built in -- `ld.so --list-diagnostics` lists them ahead of
/lib and /usr/lib -- and the installer counts them too. A distro CUDA runtime
sitting in one of those was therefore reported missing, the Ollama dir joined
LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and it displaced that runtime despite the loader probe.

Discover the dirs by glob rather than by machine name, so a multilib host, a
second architecture, or a container holding only one of the pair is covered.

The pair of arms pins it: the new discovery rule, and the real list checked
against the interpreter's own MULTIARCH triple, which is what the previous
draft asserted with a condition that could not hold.

Studio: reuse unchanged files from an older snapshot instead of re-downloading them (#11796)

* Studio: reuse unchanged files from an older snapshot instead of re-downloading them

Without symlinks (Windows without Developer Mode, FAT/exFAT, HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS)
huggingface_hub moves each downloaded blob into its snapshots/<commit>/ directory, so
blobs/ stays empty. The next commit on the Hub, even a README-only edit, then finds no
blob to link and every file of the new revision is downloaded again.

Before a download starts, the Hub download worker now looks for each expected file in
the repo's other snapshots. A regular file with the declared size whose content matches
the target commit's digest (LFS sha256, or the git blob id) is hard linked into the new
snapshot, or copied when hard links are unavailable. Content is proven by the Hub's
digest for the older commit, falling back to hashing the local file once (cached). The
diffusion download plan keeps such files staged but no longer counts their bytes.

Symlink caches are unchanged: their snapshot entries are symlinks and the blob still
exists, which huggingface_hub already reuses on its own.

* Studio: hash a reuse candidate before linking it into the new revision

The Hub reporting the same digest for the older commit proves what that commit served, not
what is on disk now, so a same-size corrupted copy was carried into the new snapshot. The
worker now always verifies the local bytes (the digest is cached, so each file is read once).
Hub digests remain only in the plan's read-only estimate.

* Studio: rehash a reuse candidate instead of trusting a cached digest

The persisted digest cache keys on size, mtime and inode, which a same-size rewrite can leave
unchanged (restored mtime, FAT/exFAT 2 s granularity, and Windows exposes no change time), so a
stale entry could carry changed bytes into the new snapshot. The worker now always hashes before
placing a file; cached digests only feed the plan's read-only estimate. POSIX keys also include
ctime_ns so those estimates miss on a restored mtime.

* Studio: check each reuse candidate's bytes once, ask the Hub lazily, and clear a killed copy

A reuse chain hard links one file into every later snapshot, so a same-size change hashed it once per snapshot. Candidates are now deduplicated by inode, the plan asks the Hub for older commits newest first and stops once every path has a match, and a temp copy left by a cancelled worker is removed before the next placement.

* Studio: leave files already in the target revision out of the disk preflight

A retry after a cancelled attempt found nothing left to reuse and asked for the size of files that attempt had already placed, which snapshot_download skips and which have no blob to discount without symlinks.

Studio: stop rewriting the compile-cache bundle on every warm start, and bound its disk use (#11874)

* Studio: stop rewriting the compile-cache bundle on every warm start, and bound its disk use

A warm start of an automatic-dynamic compile (the max tier, and torchao weights on the
default tier) re-traces every graph and inductor serves each from the cache, but the
dirty bit keyed on dynamo's graph count, so every restart rewrote the whole bundle.
Key it on FX graph cache misses instead, which only grow when inductor compiled
something the bundle does not hold.

Every key also keeps a per-key inductor dir next to its bundle and nothing ever
removed either. After a save, delete least recently used keys until the root fits
UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_COMPILE_CACHE_MAX_GB (20 GB default, 0 disables), never a key this
process has open or one used in the last hour.

* Skip the compile counter test where torch is not installed

* Compile cache: mark a key used before a render, and keep the default budget for nan/inf

* Compile cache: evict by rename after re-checking the key, count only freed bytes, enforce the budget on load

A key is re-checked for a fresh last-used stamp right before it is deleted and is then renamed out of
the key namespace, so a process opening it meanwhile sees a clean miss instead of files vanishing under
a compile; Windows refuses the rename while a file is open and the key is skipped. Only bytes actually
freed count against the budget, and leftovers are retried and counted on the next pass. A load now runs
the eviction too, since a warm hit never saves and an over-budget cache would otherwise never shrink.

* Compile cache: count a key a concurrent eviction took, and keep the default budget when the limit overflows

Losing the rename to another eviction still frees that key's bytes, so the pass no longer deletes one
more key for them. A finite limit too large to convert to bytes (1e300) fell through to an
OverflowError that abandoned every eviction pass; it now falls back to the default like nan and inf.

* perf(studio): read a forked chat's document vectors once per fork

Copying a chat's documents into its fork re-read every vector in the source thread's scope once per document inside rag.db's write transaction. vec0 scans the whole partition for any chunk filter, so a chat with 20 documents of 300 chunks held the write lock for about 34 s, well past the 5 s busy timeout of every other RAG writer. store.copy_documents now copies the set in one pass and reads each source scope's vectors once (about 2 s for the same chat).

Pointing a fork's copied citations at its own documents rewrote content_json with a bare UPDATE, which fires the attachment inventory's dirty trigger and made the next chat write rebuild the inventory for every message. body and each cell through block content controls, and follow a paragraph
with its text boxes, read once. The table layout (grid alignment, merged
cells, nested tables) is unchanged.

fix(cua-driver): keep the resting agent cursor animating on every platform (#4131)

* fix(cua-driver): keep the resting agent cursor animating on every platform

The default cursor theme levitates at rest (the shared float bob painted by
cursor_overlay::paint_cursor), but each platform decided on its own when a
settled cursor still needed frames. Only X11 kept ticking a visible resting
cursor. Native Wayland slept until the idle-fade deadline and Windows dropped
to its 250 ms idle cadence, so the bob froze for the whole idle-hide delay;
macOS froze it whenever idle hide was disabled.

copied into cursor_overlay::RenderMap: lazy creation from the template,
stable insertion z-order, tombstones, revival, the default guard, the
sentinel seed, and the frame-tick predicate. RenderStateCore::needs_frame_tick
now includes has_resting_motion(), which respects reduced motion, hidden,
faded, and off-workspace cursors, and single-frame custom themes. The
adapters keep only platform state (geometry, arrival waiters, scheduling),
and the duplicated per-platform lifecycle tests collapse into one suite.

* fix(cua-driver): let a never-hiding resting cursor quiesce the overlay

The shared resting-motion term kept a visible cursor at frame cadence for as
long as it stayed on screen. With idle hide disabled that never ends, so the
native Wayland overlay redrew full outputs at 60 fps forever and failed the
hosted wayland_overlay_quiesces_and_recovers_after_capture_and_cursor_activity
CPU certification.

while its idle-hide countdown runs and stops when the fade hides it, and a
cursor set never to hide rests still so the overlay parks. This matches the
original macOS behavior and keeps the default 20 s levitation on Windows and
Wayland.

Streamdown renders `1~10` / `~¥0.089` as GFM strikethrough pairs (two lone
tildes in one paragraph pair up and strike through the text between them),
and unknown HTML-shaped tokens like <tool_call>/<observation> are fed to
parse5 as unclosed tags, silently swallowing the rest of the message.

paths, inline & fenced code) and escape unknown html-like tokens to
entities against a 55-element safe-tag allowlist, nested into the
rewriteProseSegment pipeline that already shields URLs/file links/math.
Includes preprocess unit tests and render-level DOM regression tests.
Closes #50871, #53953.

characters; preview.act cancel (timeout or interrupt) and a local Stop both
set it, so queued keystrokes stop. A printable press on body/html is refused

test(desktop): cover the WSL bridge on every file-read boundary

The previous change wired resolveLocalReadPath into the media protocol,
readFileDataUrl, readFileText and previewFileTarget handlers inline, but
nothing locked that wiring in: dropping the bridge from any one boundary
would silently reintroduce the ENOENT on a Windows host with a WSL
backend, and wsl-path-bridge.test.ts only exercises the translation, not
the call sites (flagged by the upstream review).

Extract each boundary's path preparation into local-read-path.ts, the
same way fs-read-dir.ts already isolates the directory boundary, and have
main.ts delegate to it. The handlers keep byte-for-byte behavior; the
step is now reachable in isolation, so local-read-path.test.ts mocks
resolveLocalReadPath and asserts each boundary routes its raw path
through it (decoded media pathname, coerced IPC path, expanded-then-
bridged preview target, file: passthrough).

fix(desktop): bridge WSL paths for the remaining file-read handlers

88fbc882 added a WSL->Windows path bridge (resolveLocalReadPath) so a
Windows-hosted desktop can read a WSL backend's POSIX paths, but only wired
it into the folder-dialog defaultPath and fs-read-dir. The other IPC file
readers still hand backend-reported POSIX paths (/home/..., /mnt/c/...)
straight to resolveReadableFileForIpc / resolveRequestedPathForIpc, which
resolve them against the Windows drive (C:\home\...) and ENOENT.

On a Windows client running the backend under WSL2 in local mode this makes:
- audio/video attachments show 0:00 then fall back to "Open file" (the
  hermes-media:// stream handler 404s on the unreadable path),
- inline images / file data-url previews fail (readFileDataUrl),
- text previews fail (readFileText),
- file previews fail (previewFileTarget's existence check misses).

Extend the same bridge to those boundaries, mirroring fs-read-dir: translate
the raw path with resolveLocalReadPath before it enters the resolver. For the
preview flow the bridge runs before the fileExists() check so it sees the real
file. No-op off Windows and for already-Windows paths; the sensitive-file
blocklist still runs on the translated realpath, so file access is unchanged.

Related: #63669 (WSL inline-image routing, addressed renderer-side via the
gateway in #64074); this fixes audio/video playback and previews at the
Electron main layer, preserving native Range/seek streaming for large media.

fix(desktop): discard stale in-flight backend-update responses on profile switch

checkBackendUpdates() only guarded against concurrent calls via
$backendUpdateChecking, so switching from remote profile A to B while
A's request was still in flight caused B's trigger to be silently
skipped (locked out), and A's later response to be published
unconditionally even though B was now active. Bind each request to
the connection key active when it started, discard responses whose
key is no longer current, and queue a follow-up check for whichever
target asked for one while the lock was held.

Addresses review feedback on #62815.

fix(desktop): re-check backend updates when switching between two remote profiles

The connection-change listener in startUpdatePoller() only compared
conn.mode, which stays 'remote' when switching directly from one
remote profile to another. The pending-update indicator kept showing
the previous profile's stale result until the next 30-minute poll,
window-focus refresh, or manual check. Key on the actual backend
target (baseUrl) instead of just mode so a target change re-checks
even when the mode doesn't.

fix(desktop): track one unscoped stream pin per session

`unscopedStreamSessionId` was a single shared slot. When a second chat
started a turn while the first was still streaming, its `message.start`
overwrote the pin, and every later unscoped event from the first stream
resolved to the second chat — grafting one conversation's deltas, tool
events and reasoning onto another's transcript (#46194 / #62823).

Replace the slot with one pin per concurrent stream. `message.start` adds
a pin instead of replacing it; a stream end retires only its own pin, so
chats still streaming keep theirs.

With several streams live an unscoped event has no field naming its
owner, so it is attributed to the focused chat when that chat is itself
mid-stream, and dropped otherwise. Dropping is the conservative half:
the store keeps the correct rows, so the transcript recovers on refetch,
whereas guessing is what painted A's output onto B.

Single-stream and no-stream routing are unchanged — tightening the
no-pin fallback for late events is #70376's subject, not this change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(gateway): stop anchoring synthetic process notifications to the stale trigger message (#123097)

synthetic MessageEvent(internal=True) turns carrying the id of the message
that STARTED the process (captured at spawn time via
HERMES_SESSION_MESSAGE_ID, persisted as watcher_message_id, replayed on the
queued event). By delivery time that message is old news: the user has
typically continued elsewhere, and _reply_anchor_for_event made the finished
job's reply quote it on every reply-anchoring platform — on Discord the

fix(tui_gateway): re-place every queued row at drain, not just the dispatched one

A partial drain followed by a crash left a later-accepted prompt's
accept-time row behind the in-flight reply while the dispatched prompt's
row healed past it — permanently rendering the later prompt before the
earlier one. The drain now re-places every queued envelope's row in
acceptance order and re-slots the dispatching envelope's durable dict for
adoption (the loop would otherwise leave the last processed one in the
single slot). Regression test covers the two-image partial-drain crash;
behavioral RED first ("a later-accepted prompt rendered before an earlier
one", assert 34 < 10).

fix(tui_gateway): persist a busy-queued prompt at accept, re-place its row at turn start

A prompt accepted while the agent was busy lived only in the in-memory
queue: session.resume's cold read lacked it until its turn ran and a
backend restart lost it permanently. _handle_busy_submit now writes the
user row through the same #111868 machinery as an idle submit (extracted
as _write_submit_user_row; the durable dict rides the QUEUE ENVELOPE,
never the shared session slot the in-flight turn may own), a text-only
merge syncs the already-written row's content in place, and
_drain_queued_prompt re-places the row at the transcript end before
dispatch (fresh write + deactivate_message on the early row) so the
stored raw order stays [u, a, u, a] instead of glueing the two user
turns under repair_alternation, and the drained turn adopts the fresh
row instead of appending a duplicate. Cancel/crash keep the trailing
user row (the documented interrupted shape). display_kind rides the
envelope from prompt.submit through both writes.

(cherry picked from commit 32792f99d582608d68d40bc12930b295af0d332e)

fix(tui-gateway): reap stale deferred active-session leases (#62823 zombie slot)

When a compute-host turn has not settled by session close, the session's
real active-session lease is parked in _deferred_active_session_leases and
the turn's completion callback is supposed to release it. If that callback
is lost (supervisor restart/reload, child killed without failing its
pending turns, dropped completion), the lease sat in the registry forever:
_own_live_lease_ids vouches for it so the orphan sweep never reclaims it,
and the concurrent-session cap treats the dead session as active - new
sessions could not send until a backend restart.

Track when each lease was deferred and have the reaper tick force-release
deferred leases past a generous 30-minute ceiling (the longest legitimate
isolated turn is the compression ceiling, minutes). Normal settlement
still releases immediately and clears the age entry.

fix(tui-gateway): queue busy-mode follow-ups while compression is in flight

demotes interrupt->queue for this exact reason (gateway/run_busy.py,

classic chat share the Discord-gateway contract: prompt.submit busy
steer/interrupt and session.steer/session.redirect queue instead, and
the follow-up drains when compression finishes.

fix(mcp): budget discovery-thread GIL so agent build fits the 30s wait

Background MCP discovery does bursty CPU work (SDK/pydantic imports, JSON-RPC

out with 'agent initialization timed out' (error 5032).

Lower the interpreter switch interval while discovery runs (restored afterwards)
so its CPU bursts are sliced finely enough that waiters stay responsive.

fix(file-ops): a dangling symlink is an occupied entry, never an absent path

[ -f ] and [ -e ] follow symlinks, so a dangling link probed as missing and
read_file_raw reported not_found: V4A Add followed the link and created its
target, Move replaced the link, both reporting success. The shell size
probe, the compound read probe and the native stat now classify any
symlink entry as not a regular file.

fix(file-ops): verify the byte-exact read against the file's own byte count

The fence drops backend output around the read, not output printed while
the transport runs: a BASH_ENV DEBUG hook firing for base64 alone puts
text inside the payload that still decodes (TERM is b"LDL"), and the edit
paths wrote it back. Emit wc -c in its own fenced segment and hand bytes to
a writer only when their length matches; the od fallback is checked the
same way.

fix(file-ops): fence the binary-admission sample like the byte-exact read

Consolidates #120559 by @JoaoMarcos44 into this PR. Both PRs landed on the same
shape for #120514 — read_file_raw must be a byte-preserving mutation boundary,
framed so the backend's merged stdout is never decoded as payload — but the
sibling one step in FRONT of it was still unfenced here.

_sample_file_bytes whitespace-joined the whole reply before base64-decoding it,
so a backend that announces something on connect had that noise decoded into the
sample: "TERM" is four base64 characters and prefixes the sample with b"LDL".
That sample is the binary-admission gate read_file_raw consults, so noise there
decides whether a file is editable at all and what a refusal reports about its
bytes. Same class as the read this PR already fixed, one call earlier.

_fenced_read() is that framing extracted once — sentinel, payload segment, and
the body's own exit status in its own trailing segment — and the three byte
transports (sample, base64, od fallback) now share it instead of repeating the
split/parse/decode triplet, with _failed_read() for the diagnostic they all
surfaced by hand.

The mock double for the sample transport moves to the fenced reply shape the
other doubles in that file already build, so it stays honest about the fence.

Co-authored-by: JoaoMarcos44 <joaomarcosdias444@gmail.com>
test(file-ops): gate the FIFO read test to hosts with os.mkfifo

fix(patch): a Move or Add destination is free only when its read says absent

Validation treated every read_file_raw error as "the path is free" for an
Add target and a Move destination; only _apply_add checked not_found. With no
byte transport (native reads off, no base64 or od) an `Add new-src` then
`Move new-src -> dst` validated, and the mv replaced the existing dst while
the patch reported success.

_occupied() frees a path only on not_found (overlay-aware), and _apply_move
re-checks the destination right before mv, since validation's answer is stale
once earlier ops of the patch have applied.

fix(file-ops): a failed byte-exact read is not an absent file

Three defects in the byte-exact read this PR introduced.

base64 is not on every backend (busybox, distroless). The sample path
already degrades when it is missing; this one returned the read as a
failure, and read_file_raw is also _apply_add's existence check, which
treated any error as "the path is free". A backend with cat but no base64
turned `*** Add File` over an existing file into a silent overwrite that
reported success:

    main:     refused, "file already exists — use Update File"
    PR head:  b'KEEP ME -- months of work\n' -> b'clobbered by Add'

So: fall back to od (POSIX, in busybox) when base64 exits 127, and when
neither exists report a transport error. ReadResult grows not_found, set
only where the path is genuinely absent, and _apply_add refuses unless it
sees that flag — a read that FAILED can no longer pass as an absent path.
getattr keeps a producer without the field failing closed rather than
raising. The doubles in test_patch_parser that meant "absent" now say so.

The native fast path stat'd the path and then opened it, two lookups on a
name. A swap to a FIFO in between blocks the thread, and nothing times out
that. One O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK open, fstat on THAT descriptor, then read, so
a non-regular file is handed to the shell path and its timeout instead.

Tests: the od fallback round-trips byte-exactly and patches; an Add over a
file the backend cannot read is refused with the file intact; the native
read hands a FIFO to the shell rather than opening it. The first two go red
if their fix is removed. The third pins the property, not the race — with
one descriptor there is no window left to swap into, so reverting to
stat-then-open does not flip it.

Not addressed here: inserted text is still encoded UTF-8 regardless of the
file's declared encoding, so an edit adding non-ASCII to a latin-1 file
writes mixed bytes. That is the write half, it predates this PR, and it
needs source-encoding detection.

fix(file-ops): fence the byte-exact read so backend stdout noise is not decoded

The byte-exact read whitespace-joined the whole reply before decoding, so
anything a backend prepends to its merged stdout became part of the base64.
A remote shell announcing TERM is four base64 characters, which decodes to
b"LDL" and lands at the head of the file the edit paths then write back:
patching HEADER\nVERSION=1\n left LDLHEADER\nVERSION=2\n on disk.

Fence the payload between a per-call sentinel, the shape the compound read
probe already uses and for the same reason. _new_sentinel's underscores are
outside the base64 alphabet, so noise that lands inside the fence fails
validation instead of decoding into bytes, and noise outside it is dropped.
The read's exit status rides in its own trailing segment, so a failed read
is still told apart from an empty file without && chaining or exit.

stderr stays merged rather than silenced: on a failed read that segment
carries the backend's own diagnostic ("No such file or directory"), which
the callers surface, and a reply with no fence at all hands the backend's
text straight back so a wrapper cd failure still reports itself.

The two doubles this PR added keyed off the old command string; they now
build a fenced reply from the sentinel in the command they were handed, so
they stay honest about the fence the transport depends on.

The new test drives the noisy backend through the real transport: the
existing tests use LocalEnvironment, which takes the native read path on
POSIX and never exercises base64 at all.

fix(file-ops): both patch modes read their write-back source byte-exactly

Review follow-up (ehz0ah, teknium1). Keying the cleanup on the
__HERMES_FENCE_ marker still rewrote a real line that contains that
text, and nothing has emitted the wrapper since the spawn-per-call layer
(d684d7ee7e), so the cleanup can only ever eat the file's own bytes.

The same class also hit mode="replace", the default: patch_replace (and
V4A past the 1000-byte binary sample) read the file through the text
transport, which decodes with errors="replace", so any byte UTF-8 cannot
decode came back as U+FFFD and was persisted on lines the edit never
touched, while the diff and the post-write check (same lossy read) showed
nothing.

_read_exact_bytes reads natively on the local POSIX host (regular files
only) and over base64 elsewhere; read_file_raw, patch_replace and
_verify_patch_persisted decode it with surrogateescape, which write_file's
encode already inverts (#79178), so every untouched byte is written back
exactly and no readable file becomes a read error (V4A's Add/Move/Delete
existence checks are unchanged). A garbled transport reply refuses
instead of writing stray output into the file. The Python linter parses
bytes so a declared legacy coding still lints clean. Local edits spawn
two fewer shells (replace 5 -> 3, V4A 9 -> 7).

fix(file-ops): a V4A patch keeps terminal escape bytes on lines it never touched

read_file_raw feeds the V4A write-back, and it ran the whole file through the
terminal fence-leak cleanup, which deletes every OSC sequence and BEL byte. A
prompt script's title escape or a beep line was silently rewritten on apply, and
the diff and post-write hash both started from the stripped text, so nothing
showed it. A leaked wrapper always carries the fence marker: clean only those
lines when the content is going to be written back.

On Windows, subprocess text=True without an explicit encoding decodes

raise UnicodeDecodeError inside subprocess._readerthread, killing the

timeout.

errors='replace', and add an AST-based regression test that fails when a

fix(update): stop reading gateway identity off the Windows restart watcher's argv (#107002) (#121635)

* fix(update): stop reading gateway identity off the restart watcher's argv (#107002)

The detached restart watcher is spawned as
`python -c <watcher source> <old_pid> <python> -m hermes_cli.main gateway run`.
Its trailing argv is the command it will spawn LATER, but the canonical matchers
read identity straight off the joined command line, so the watcher itself was
classified as a live `gateway run` process — the documented "never infer process
identity from argv substrings" bug class, on the exact surface `hermes update`
uses to verify a post-update relaunch.

Also budget the post-relaunch liveness poll against the watcher's own deadline:
the watcher respawns the gateway only after the PID it was handed exits, so a
30 s window can expire before the relaunch it verifies was scheduled to start.

* test(windows-live): run the gateway-ancestor harness parent from a script file

A `python -c <src>` parent is an interpreter running inline source and carries
no readable Hermes identity, so it is no longer a gateway to any classifier —
the harness's own comment already said a realistic gateway argv is not a -c blob.

* test(windows-live): share one sleeper SCRIPT across the live process-topology fixtures

Four live Windows E2E files stood processes up as `python -c "sleep" <hermes argv tail>`.
That shape no longer carries a readable Hermes identity, so the fixtures stopped standing
in for the gateways they simulate. One shared sleeper script replaces the -c spelling.

* fix(gateway): drop the duplicated _INLINE_SOURCE_FLAG_RE definition

The constant was emitted twice around command_line_runs_inline_source. Same
pattern both times, so behaviour is unchanged — but one definition is enough.

* test(stderr-timestamp): run the gateway-lookalike children from script files

Both lookalikes stood a gateway child up as `python -c <src> <gateway tail>`.
That shape no longer carries a readable Hermes identity (#107002), so the
wrapper correctly stopped treating them as gateway spawns and the tests failed.
A `-c` tail is data for a program the inline source may spawn LATER, never the
child's own identity — the real wrapper child is `python -m hermes_cli.main
gateway run`, which has no `-c`. Running the stand-ins from a real script file
restores what the tests mean to assert without depending on the misread.

fix(serve): retire an SSH-isolated backend once the install moves to new code

The serve a remote Desktop spawns over SSH is never restarted by the
host's updater (only its client holds the token and owner nonce), and
the idle watchdog stays quiet while that client is connected. After an
update it therefore kept running the pre-update code against the new
tree until the client happened to reconnect.

Poll the checkout sha against the sha this process loaded. On two
consecutive mismatches, with no update in flight, retire through the
existing retirement fence (which proves idle and closes admission), and
exit cleanly so the client respawns the backend on the new code. Unknown
shas, busy or unreadable ledgers and a live update all keep it up.

inventory read it as manual-serve: an update filed a manual-restart

as unaccounted, and abort recovery could try an argv respawn without the
client's token file and owner nonce.

Classify it as desktop-ssh (using the canonical argv predicate, so rows
written before the ledger carried isolated are covered too) and treat it
like the local Desktop's own serve: skipped by the restart phase,
deferred to its client, never owed by abort recovery. A hand-started
serve --isolated stays manual-serve.

attach-first discovery adopted it. Nothing on this host owns that

fix(api): flush the SSE head before waiting for the first run event

`_handle_run_events` called `response.prepare(request)` and went straight
into the queue wait without writing a byte. aiohttp keeps the response head
in the socket buffer until the first body write, so a client that subscribes
before the run emits anything receives no headers at all — `fetch()` and
`EventSource` never resolve and the stream looks dead rather than connected.

The approval flow is the worst case. `approval.request` is only emitted once
the model has thought about the turn, routinely 20-60s, and a UI that
subscribes right after `POST /v1/runs` is supposed to be showing "connected"
that whole time. Instead it has nothing: no status, no headers, no way to
tell a live stream from a hung one. Absent any event, the first write is the
30s keepalive, so that is the ceiling on time-to-first-byte.

Write a single SSE comment frame right after `prepare()`. Comment lines are
ignored by every conforming consumer — `EventSource` dispatches nothing for
them — so this changes the head's arrival time and nothing else.

Scoped to the reported handler. Three sibling streams in this file
(chat-completions and the two responses streams) share the shape; they write
their first frame promptly enough that the same wait has not been reported
against them, and widening a latency fix into them without that evidence
would be guessing.

Tests drive the real handler over aiohttp's TestClient with a registered run
whose queue never fills — the exact "subscribed before the first event"
shape. On unpatched main the first-byte read times out; with the flush it
returns immediately. A second test pins that the preamble stays a comment, so
no consumer can mistake it for an event.

fix(slack): never re-post a successfully streamed answer

Problem: with native streaming (chat.startStream/appendStream/stopStream)
the same answer could land twice in a thread — once as the streamed
message, once as a fresh chat.postMessage — while the streamed message
kept its live-typing indicator.

Mechanism: `_try_finalize_stream` matched the turn-final against the
streamed text with a raw `startswith`. The agent strips `final_response`
and joins footers with `rstrip()`, so any surrounding-whitespace
difference made the finalize fall through to a plain post although the
open stream already showed the whole answer (and was never sealed). A
`chat.stopStream` failure took the same fresh-post path even when the
streamed text equalled the final. Streams were also keyed per `chat_id`
only, so two concurrent turns in two threads of one channel sealed or
overwrote each other's stream.

Fix:
- Key native streams per `(team_id, chat_id, thread_ts)`; the stream
  consumer stamps the same `thread_id` on every draft frame and on the
  turn-final `send()`, so both resolve to the same key.
- Honor the streaming contract (gateway/AGENTS.md): sends carrying
  `_interim_send` or `expect_edits` never seal a stream.
- Classify the final against the streamed text as equal / extends /
  unrelated with edge-whitespace tolerance (`_stream_relation`). The
  stopStream delta is sliced from the RAW final, so nothing inside the
  answer (blank lines, fences, tables) is dropped or repeated.
- Commit rule: one `chat.stopStream`, one retry only when no tail is
  appended (`markdown_text` APPENDS, so an ambiguous failure must not
  repeat it), then `edit_message(finalize=True)` on the stream ts as the
  idempotent in-place commit — it already owns format/truncate/Block Kit
  and the block-rejection retry. Only when both fail does `send()` post
  a fresh message (a duplicate beats a lost answer).
- Oversized tails and rewritten finals (`notify=True`) seal the stale
  stream on what is visible before falling back, so no stream is left
  with a live-typing indicator.
- `_seal_stream` takes the exact unsent delta instead of recomputing it
  from `final_text`; `disconnect()` and the stream API calls route
  through the stream's own team client.

Tests: tests/gateway/test_slack_native_streaming.py covers the
whitespace-only difference, the stopStream-failure commit path, the
bounded retry, the uncommittable fallback, interim/preview sends,
per-thread keying, oversized tails, rewritten finals and the
GatewayStreamConsumer end-to-end path.

fix(desktop): keep continuous voice working after a mic meter AudioContext error (#122278)

* fix(desktop): wait for the last mic meter to close and report a dead one

The voice recorder's level meter fired AudioContext.close() without awaiting
it and opened a new context on every take, so back-to-back takes (and the
barge-in monitor) could hold two capture contexts at once. That is what makes
Chromium raise "The AudioContext encountered an error from the audio device",
and the error was never handled: the analyser went flat and the take read as
silence.

Meter closes now go through mic-meter-context, and both the recorder and the
barge monitor wait for pending closes (capped at 1s) before opening a new
context. The recorder watches its context for 'error' and an unexpected
'closed', treats a context it can't build as failed, calls
onMeterFailure, and marks the take meterFailed.

* fix(desktop): transcribe voice turns whose level meter died

Continuous voice dropped any take whose meter-only heardSpeech stayed false,
so once the AudioContext errored every later utterance was discarded before
STT with no error shown. A meter failure now ends the turn, and the take goes
to STT unless it is under 750ms (STT decides whether there was speech).
Back-to-back meter failures show "Microphone failed" and end the conversation
instead of re-arming forever.

reports success, and posix.sh swaps the install's stale release/ build
back over the app. Pressing Update can never get out of that loop.

`hermes update` now notices it is running on another checkout's in-tree
venv and re-runs itself with that install's own code (PYTHONPATH=<install>,
cwd=<install>). The install's updater pulls the install and reinstalls it
into its venv, which points the editable record home again, so the next
relaunch runs a fresh build. A wrapper that put the running checkout on
PYTHONPATH on purpose chose that tree and is left alone.

fix(pm): never adopt another install's venv for a checkout

project_venv_dir() fell back to the running interpreter's venv whenever
hermes_constants was loaded from the checkout. Where the code was loaded
from says nothing about who owns the interpreter: with
`PYTHONPATH=<dev checkout> <app install>/venv/bin/python -m hermes_cli.main`
(a shell wrapper around a dev tree), PROJECT_ROOT is the dev checkout but
the venv is the Desktop install's. base_venv() then returned the app's
venv, `hermes update` synced the dev tree into it, and the Desktop
install's venv became an editable install of the dev checkout. From then
on the Desktop shell tracked ~/.hermes/hermes-agent while its backend and
its handed-off `hermes update` ran and pulled the dev tree, so every
in-app update "succeeded" without moving the install. The same misread
let running_from_selected_environment() accept lazy extras into that
venv.

Only fall back to the running venv when its own hermes-agent install
records this checkout in direct_url.json, which every install of a
checkout into a venv writes (installers, uv sync). Otherwise the
checkout gets its own environment, as it did before 4f6c04cd07. The
#116148 out-of-tree layout (a venv installed from the checkout) still
resolves to the running interpreter.

fix(desktop): never resolve a source root's interpreter off PATH

findPythonForRoot ended in findSystemPython(), so a checkout with no
in-tree venv/.venv produced a PATH Python. Two designed refusals were
therefore unreachable: readSourceUpdate's `!managed && !probe.python`
guard (checkout-source.ts) and StateDbPreflight's `string | null` python
plus its "Python not found" throw (state-db-preflight.ts). Both were
written expecting null and could never see it.

A PATH Python can import a checkout while lacking its selected
dependencies, which is the failure the checkout-source comment already
names, so a failed read became a wrong answer instead of a refusal:
the update probe, the state.db pre-flight and the source backend all
ran under an interpreter nothing selected. PM deletes the in-tree
venv/.venv once a generation is committed, making null the ordinary
answer for a managed install — its callers resolve the installation
launcher instead, and the backend ladder falls through to its next rung.

resolveSourcePython owns the decision (override, then the checkout's own
venv, else null) and findPythonForRoot keeps its signature, so the four
call sites are unchanged. findSystemPython stays for the uninstaller,
whose interpreter choice is a separate, deliberate one for a locked venv.

So `gateway start --all` from the new checkout still saw an interactive
console, asked "Install it now so the gateway starts on login?" into
the captured stdout, and waited forever. The update never relaunched.

a question they cannot see.

Merge pull request #122154 from NousResearch/fix/record-powershell-args

test(desktop-update): read the console self-test report as UTF-16

Windows PowerShell 5.1 `*>` writes UTF-16LE with a BOM. Decoding it as
UTF-8 hid the PASS line even though the self-test exited 0.

fix(pm): retry a plugin fetch failure once, then disable it

Sitting a plugin out after a fetch failure left the recorded stamp stale on
purpose, so every launch resynced, and the spawned-process guard in
prepare_launch raised "dependency sync left this install out of date".
One retry covers a blip; after that the plugin is disabled with the reason,
and hermes plugins enable restores it. Only requires_hermes still sits out,
which boot skips the same way.

fix(pm): keep the manifest import per plugin; pin the version in the sit-out test

enabled_member_dirs imported hermes_cli.plugins_manifest before its loop, so a
PM closure with no plugins selected needed the application's utils module
(tests/scripts/test_source_driver.py builds exactly that tree).

The requires_hermes sit-out test relied on the host's version identity. A
tagless CI checkout has no parseable version, which makes the gate permissive.

fix(pm): disable a plugin only on evidence about the plugin

An update disabled any plugin that failed a trial build or its
requires_hermes check. Both can be about us, not the plugin: an untagged
source checkout reads as an older release (#122054), so requires_hermes
misjudges a fine plugin, and a download failure says nothing about the
plugin's code. Those now sit the plugin out of the build: config stays
untouched and it rejoins once the cause clears.

Disabling still happens on evidence about the plugin: requires-python vs
the pinned interpreter, manifest_version, an invalid declaration, a uv
resolution conflict, or its own build backend failing (new BuildFailure,
keyed on uv's 'The build backend returned an error').

enabled_member_dirs now skips a requires_hermes misfit instead of
raising. Boot's currency check raised on it before any sync could run, so
the launch path never reached the update sync. The loader skips such a
plugin anyway; admission still refuses enabling one.

fix(pm): an unreadable secondary profile config cannot fail an update

Venv.apply refused the whole graph when any secondary profile's
config.yaml was unreadable, so one broken sibling config failed every
update. Update syncs now leave that profile's plugins out of the union,
report it (stderr + receipt warning), and build the rest; the profile's
plugins rejoin on the next sync once its config is fixed. Boot currency
already skips broken secondaries, so the result reads as current.
Ordinary syncs keep refusing to shrink the recorded graph.

fix(pm): disable plugins that no longer fit instead of failing the update

An update resolves the enabled plugin union against the NEW core. A plugin
admitted against the old core can stop fitting when core moves (managed
Python 3.13 -> 3.14 vs a member's requires-python <3.14, a requires_hermes
upper bound, a bumped pin), and the whole update then died after the
source swap with a non-resolver InstallError whose 'retry' hint failed the
same way every time.

Update syncs now pass evict_incompatible_plugins=True (update completion,
historical takeover, launch-time completion, venv_sync, post-update
drift). PM screens statically first (requires-python vs the target
interpreter, manifest/requires_hermes), then, if the rest still fails,
builds core alone to prove the plugins are the cause and re-adds members
in config order, disabling each one that breaks the build. Misfits land in
plugins.disabled (memory.provider cleared) in every home that enables
them, published through the existing journaled change hook (the journal
now carries several configs), and are reported on stderr + receipt
warnings. Admission and ordinary syncs still refuse; only a core that
cannot build on its own fails an update.
fix: restore upstream behavior lost in PM conflict resolutions
